review.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requisite for the use of the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The injury suffered must not be due to any voluntary action of the person who suffered the injury.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard of medical care must be discussed by an expert in court.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The instrumentality which caused the injury was under the control of the person in charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent.

review.explanation: This statement is incorrect. The doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur does not necessarily require the standard of care to be discussed by a medical expert in court. Instead, it relies on the presumption of negligence based on the circumstances surrounding the injury. While expert testimony may support the application of Res Ipsa Loquitur by providing insight into the standard of care, it is not a strict requirement for its application.

choiceRationales.A: This statement aligns with the principle of Res Ipsa Loquitur, which translates to "the thing speaks for itself." It implies that the injury or harm sustained must not have resulted from any voluntary action or contribution by the individual who suffered the injury. Res Ipsa Loquitur applies when the injured party did not play a role in causing the harm and could not have prevented it through their actions.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is incorrect. The doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur does not necessarily require the standard of care to be discussed by a medical expert in court. Instead, it relies on the presumption of negligence based on the circumstances surrounding the injury. While expert testimony may support the application of Res Ipsa Loquitur by providing insight into the standard of care, it is not a strict requirement for its application.
choiceRationales.C: Under the doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur, the instrumentality or object that caused the injury must have been under the control or management of the defendant at the time of the incident. This control element is essential because it helps establish that the defendant had the responsibility and ability to prevent the harm that occurred.
choiceRationales.D: This statement reflects another key aspect of Res Ipsa Loquitur. It suggests that the nature of the accident or injury is such that it typically does not happen in the absence of negligence. The occurrence of the accident itself implies that negligence likely played a role, given the circumstances and the control of the instrumentality by the defendant.

review.stem: The MOST consistent cause of osteomyelitis is which one of the following organisms?
review.explanation:
Osteomyelitis, an infection of bone, can be caused by various microorganisms that arrive at bone through different routes. Spontaneous hematogenous osteomyelitis may occur in otherwise healthy individuals, whereas local microbial spread mainly affects either individuals who have underlying disease (e.g., vascular insufficiency) or patients who have compromised skin or other tissue barriers, with consequent exposure of bone. The latter situation typically follows surgery involving bone, such as sternotomy or orthopedic repair.
The great majority of cases are monomicrobial in etiology. Of episodes of acute vertebral osteomyelitis, 40–50% are caused by Staphylococcus aureus, 12% by streptococci, and 20% by gram-negative bacilli—mainly Escherichia coli (9%) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (6%). Subacute vertebral osteomyelitis is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella species in regions where these microorganisms are endemic.

choiceRationales.A: Escherichia coli is as a cause of osteomyelitis, particularly in the context of acute vertebral osteomyelitis. It is responsible for a proportion of cases, with around 9% attributed to E. coli. However, the MOST consistent cause is Staphylococcus aureus.
choiceRationales.B: Klebsiella is not a primary cause of osteomyelitis. The most consistent cause, especially in acute vertebral osteomyelitis, is Staphylococcus aureus.
choiceRationales.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a cause of osteomyelitis, accounting for around 6% of cases of acute vertebral osteomyelitis. While it is significant, the MOST consistent cause, according to the information provided, is Staphylococcus aureus.
choiceRationales.D:
Osteomyelitis, an infection of bone, can be caused by various microorganisms that arrive at bone through different routes. Spontaneous hematogenous osteomyelitis may occur in otherwise healthy individuals, whereas local microbial spread mainly affects either individuals who have underlying disease (e.g., vascular insufficiency) or patients who have compromised skin or other tissue barriers, with consequent exposure of bone. The latter situation typically follows surgery involving bone, such as sternotomy or orthopedic repair.

Subacute vertebral osteomyelitis is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella species in regions where these microorganisms are endemic.

review.stem: Which antibody titers indicate recent or recurrent streptococcal infection and are found MOST OFTEN in rheumatic individuals?
review.explanation:
Streptolysin O is an immunogenic, beta-hemolysin. Antibody to Streptolysin O is a marker of recent mucosal infections used in the diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease (ASO titer) along with clinical symptoms. An elevated titer is also proof of a previous streptococcal infection. It is usually more elevated after a pharyngeal than skin infection, while the ADB is typically elevated regardless of the site of the infection.
M proteins are anchored in Strep. pyogenes’ cytoplasmic membrane with Class I M proteins extending through the cell wall to the cell surface although Class II M proteins do not. Strains causing rheumatic heart disease have exposed Class I M proteins, which are responsible for cross-reactivity with human heart antigens.

Antibody to Streptolysin O is a marker of recent mucosal infections used in the diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease (ASO titer) along with clinical symptoms. An elevated titer is also proof of a previous streptococcal infection. It is usually more elevated after a pharyngeal than skin infection, while the ADB is typically elevated regardless of the site of the infection.
M proteins are anchored in Strep. pyogenes’ cytoplasmic membrane with Class I M proteins extending through the cell wall to the cell surface although Class II M proteins do not. choiceRationales.B: Anti-hyaluronidase antibodies are not typically used as markers for streptococcal infections or rheumatic disease. choiceRationales.D: M proteins are surface proteins of Streptococcus pyogenes. While M proteins play a role in the pathogenesis of streptococcal infections, including rheumatic fever, measuring anti-M protein antibodies is not a common practice for routine diagnosis or monitoring. ASO and anti-DNase B antibodies are more commonly used in this context.

review.stem: In which of the following exudate specimen can a positive smear for Neisseria gonorrhea be a basis for presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea and start of treatment without additional laboratory test/s?
review.explanation:
A Suggestive diagnosis is defined by the presence of:
1.) a mucopurulent endocervical or urethral exudate on physical examination
2.) sexual exposure to a person infected with N. gonorrhoeae.
A Presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea is made on the basis of one of the following three criteria:
1.) typical gram-negative intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination of a smear of urethral exudate from men or endocervical secretions from women
2.) growth of a gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus, from the urethra (men) or endocervix (women), on a selective culture medium, and demonstration of typical colonial morphology, positive oxidase reaction, and typical gram-negative morphology
3.) detection of N. gonorrhoeae by a nonculture laboratory test (Antigen detection test, direct specimen nucleic acid probe test, nucleic acid amplification test).
The observation of gram-negative, intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination of endocervical secretions from women must be supported by a positive result from a test from either 2 or 3 to make a laboratory diagnosis of "presumptive N. gonorrhoeae."
A Definitive diagnosis of gonorrhea requires:
1.) isolation of N. gonorrhoeae from sites of exposure (e.g., urethra, endocervix, throat, rectum) by culture (usually a selective medium) and demonstrating typical colonial morphology, positive oxidase reaction, and typical gram-negative morphology
2.) confirmation of isolates by biochemical, enzymatic, serologic, or nucleic acid testing (e.g., carbohydrate utilization, rapid enzyme substrate tests, serologic methods such as coagglutination or fluorescent antibody tests supplemented with additional tests that will ensure accurate identification of isolates, or a DNA probe culture confirmation technique).

choiceRationales.A: A positive smear for Neisseria gonorrhoeae in the throat is not sufficient for a presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea without additional laboratory tests. The criteria for a presumptive diagnosis typically involve the observation of typical gram-negative intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination, growth of N. gonorrhoeae on a selective culture medium, or detection by a nonculture laboratory test.
choiceRationales.B:
A positive smear for Neisseria gonorrhea in an endocervical specimen can be a basis for a presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea. The presence of typical gram-negative intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination meets one of the criteria for a presumptive diagnosis. However, this observation must be supported by additional tests, such as a culture or nonculture laboratory test, to make a definitive diagnosis.
The uterine cervix is the most common site of mucosal infection with N. gonorrhoeae in females.
choiceRationales.C:
A Suggestive diagnosis is defined by the presence of:
1.) a mucopurulent endocervical or urethral exudate on physical examination
2.) sexual exposure to a person infected with N. gonorrhoeae.
A Presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea is made on the basis of one of the following three criteria:

2.) growth of a gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus, from the urethra (men) or endocervix (women), on a selective culture medium, and demonstration of typical colonial morphology, positive oxidase reaction, and typical gram-negative morphology
3.) detection of N. gonorrhoeae by a nonculture laboratory test (Antigen detection test, direct specimen nucleic acid probe test, nucleic acid amplification test).
The observation of gram-negative, intracellular diplococci on microscopic examination of endocervical secretions from women must be supported by a positive result from a test from either 2 or 3 to make a laboratory diagnosis of "presumptive N. gonorrhoeae."
A Definitive diagnosis of gonorrhea requires:
1.) isolation of N. gonorrhoeae from sites of exposure (e.g., urethra, endocervix, throat, rectum) by culture (usually a selective medium) and demonstrating typical colonial morphology, positive oxidase reaction, and typical gram-negative morphology
2.) confirmation of isolates by biochemical, enzymatic, serologic, or nucleic acid testing (e.g., carbohydrate utilization, rapid enzyme substrate tests, serologic methods such as coagglutination or fluorescent antibody tests supplemented with additional tests that will ensure accurate identification of isolates, or a DNA probe culture confirmation technique).
choiceRationales.D: A positive smear for Neisseria gonorrhoeae in the rectum alone is not sufficient for a presumptive diagnosis of gonorrhea. The criteria for presumptive diagnosis typically involve the presence of a mucopurulent endocervical or urethral exudate on physical examination, along with sexual exposure to an infected individual. The observation of gram-negative intracellular diplococci in the rectum must be supported by additional laboratory tests, such as culture or nonculture tests, to make a presumptive diagnosis

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: What is the MOST APPROPRIATE statement regarding the Herpes Simplex Virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the presence of intact skin, the route of infection is either oral or the genital mucosa only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latent infection follows the primary infection with the virus persisting in the ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Newborns who acquire passively maternal antibodies are permanently protected from viral infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibodies from a primary infection prevent recurrence of the infection

review.explanation:
HSV is transmitted by contact of a susceptible person with an individual excreting virus. The virus must encounter mucosal surfaces or broken skin for an infection to be initiated (unbroken skin is resistant). Viral replication occurs first at the site of infection. Virus then invades local nerve endings and is transported by retrograde axonal flow to dorsal root ganglia, where, after further replication, latency is established.
Provoactive stimuli can reactivate virus from the latent state, including axonal injury, fever, physical or emotional stress, and exposure to ultraviolet light. The virus follows axons back to the peripheral site, and replication proceeds at the skin or mucous membranes. Spontaneous reactivations occur despite HSV-specific humoral and cellular immunity in the host. However, this immunity limits local viral replication, so that recurrent infections are less extensive and less severe.
Many newborns acquire passively transferred maternal antibodies. These antibodies are lost during the first 6 months of life, and the period of greatest susceptibility to primary herpes infection occurs between ages 6 months and 2 years. Transplacentally acquired antibodies from the mother are not totally protective against infection of newborns, but they seem to ameliorate infection if not prevent it.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is not entirely accurate. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) can infect mucosal surfaces or broken skin. Unbroken skin is generally resistant to infection, but if there are breaks or lesions, the virus can initiate an infection. The virus can enter through oral or genital mucosa, but it can also infect other areas with compromised skin.
choiceRationales.B:
HSV is transmitted by contact of a susceptible person with an individual excreting virus. The virus must encounter mucosal surfaces or broken skin for an infection to be initiated (unbroken skin is resistant). Viral replication occurs first at the site of infection. Virus then invades local nerve endings and is transported by retrograde axonal flow to dorsal root ganglia, where, after further replication, latency is established.
Provoactive stimuli can reactivate virus from the latent state, including axonal injury, fever, physical or emotional stress, and exposure to ultraviolet light. The virus follows axons back to the peripheral site, and replication proceeds at the skin or mucous membranes. Spontaneous reactivations occur despite HSV-specific humoral and cellular immunity in the host. However, this immunity limits local viral replication, so that recurrent infections are less extensive and less severe.
Many newborns acquire passively transferred maternal antibodies. These antibodies are lost during the first 6 months of life, and the period of greatest susceptibility to primary herpes infection occurs between ages 6 months and 2 years. Transplacentally acquired antibodies from the mother are not totally protective against infection of newborns, but they seem to ameliorate infection if not prevent it.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is not accurate. While newborns can acquire passively transferred maternal antibodies, these antibodies are not permanent protection against HSV infection. Maternally acquired antibodies are gradually lost during the first 6 months of life, and susceptibility to primary herpes infection is greatest between 6 months and 2 years of age.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is partially accurate. While antibodies generated from a primary infection with HSV can contribute to limiting the severity and extent of recurrent infections, they do not entirely prevent recurrence. Spontaneous reactivations of the virus can occur despite the presence of HSV-specific humoral and cellular immunity.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: Which is the most common viral infection of the reproductive system?
review.explanation: Human papillomaviruses are the most common sexually transmitted viruses and include strains that cause genital warts as well as strains that cause cervical cancer. Several strains of HPV cause venereal warts, the most common STD. Some types (most commonly 16 and 18) are also associated with cervical dysplasia and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.

choiceRationales.A: Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus. It primarily affects the skin and mucous membranes, including the genital area. While it can be sexually transmitted, it is not as common in the reproductive system as other viral infections. It typically presents as small, raised, and painless bumps on the skin.
choiceRationales.B: HIV is a virus that primarily targets the immune system, leading to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). While HIV can be transmitted through sexual contact, it affects the immune system rather than causing visible lesions or symptoms in the reproductive system. It is a serious and life-threatening infection that can lead to various complications if not managed properly.
choiceRationales.C: Human papillomaviruses are the most common sexually transmitted viruses and include strains that cause genital warts as well as strains that cause cervical cancer. Several strains of HPV cause venereal warts, the most common STD. Some types (most commonly 16 and 18) are also associated with cervical dysplasia and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
choiceRationales.D: Genital herpes is caused by the herpes simplex virus (HSV) and is a common sexually transmitted infection. HSV type 2 is more commonly associated with genital herpes, while HSV type 1 can also cause genital infections. It presents with painful sores or blisters in the genital area and can recur periodically.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: To which of the following is the toxicity in gonococcal infection largely attributed to?
review.explanation:
In contrast to the enteric gram-negative rods, gonococcal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) does not have long O-antigen side chains and is called a lipooligosaccharide (LOS). Its MW is 3–7 kDa. Gonococci can express more than one antigenically different LOS chain simultaneously.
Toxicity in gonococcal infections is largely attributable to the endotoxic effects of LOS. Specifically, in the fallopian tube explant model, LOS causes ciliary loss and mucosal cell death.

choiceRationales.A:
In contrast to the enteric gram-negative rods, gonococcal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) does not have long O-antigen side chains and is called a lipooligosaccharide (LOS). Its MW is 3–7 kDa. Gonococci can express more than one antigenically different LOS chain simultaneously.
Toxicity in gonococcal infections is largely attributable to the endotoxic effects of LOS. Specifically, in the fallopian tube explant model, LOS causes ciliary loss and mucosal cell death.
choiceRationales.B: Gonococci express hairlike appendages called fimbriae or pili. These structures extend from the gonococcal surface and play a crucial role in enhancing attachment to host cells and resisting phagocytosis. While important for attachment, fimbriae are not the primary contributors to the toxicity associated with gonococcal infections.
choiceRationales.C: Opa proteins are involved in the adhesion of gonococci within colonies and attachment to host cell receptors, such as heparin-related compounds and CD66 or carcinoembryonic antigen–related cell adhesion molecules. They contribute to the pathogenicity of gonococcal infections by facilitating adhesion to host cells, but they are not the primary source of toxicity.
choiceRationales.D: Por protein is another component of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. It extends through the gonococcal cell membrane and forms pores in the surface, allowing some nutrients to enter the cell. Por proteins may impact intracellular killing of gonococci within neutrophils by preventing phagosomelysosome fusion. The variable resistance of gonococci to killing by normal human serum depends on whether Por protein selectively binds to complement components C3b and C4b.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: What is the major problem posed by infection with enterococci (E. faecalis and E. faecium)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They can be very resistant to antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several species of the organism are associated with disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: It can be transmitted to patients from the hands of hospital personnel

choices.label: D
choices.text: They grow well in environments with a wide range temperature

review.explanation: Enterococci have the potential for resistance to virtually all clinically useful antibiotics. Their emergence as important nosocomial pathogens has coincided with increased expression of antimicrobial resistance by members of the genus. The mechanisms underlying antibiotic resistance in enterococci may be intrinsic to the species or acquired through mutation of intrinsic genes or horizontal exchange of genetic material encoding resistance determinants.

choiceRationales.A: Enterococci have the potential for resistance to virtually all clinically useful antibiotics. Their emergence as important nosocomial pathogens has coincided with increased expression of antimicrobial resistance by members of the genus. The mechanisms underlying antibiotic resistance in enterococci may be intrinsic to the species or acquired through mutation of intrinsic genes or horizontal exchange of genetic material encoding resistance determinants.
choiceRationales.B: Enterococci, particularly E. faecalis and E. faecium, are associated with various infections in humans. They can cause urinary tract infections, bloodstream infections, intra-abdominal infections, endocarditis, and other serious infections. While the ability to cause disease is a concern, the major clinical challenge is often the antibiotic resistance exhibited by these organisms.
choiceRationales.C: Enterococci can be transmitted to patients from the hands of hospital personnel, contributing to their role as nosocomial pathogens. In healthcare settings, the transmission of enterococci between patients, via contaminated hands or surfaces, can lead to the spread of these bacteria. This emphasizes the importance of infection control measures to prevent healthcare-associated infections.
choiceRationales.D: Enterococci are resilient bacteria that can grow in various environmental conditions. While their ability to thrive in different temperature ranges is noteworthy, the major clinical concern is their resistance to antibiotics rather than their growth characteristics.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: What diagnostic procedure can be done which will be strongly suggestive of endocarditis?
review.explanation: Infective endocarditis is life-threatening; identification of the underlying etiology informs optimized individual patient management. Changing epidemiology, advances in blood culture techniques, and new diagnostics guide the application of laboratory testing for diagnosis of endocarditis. Blood cultures remain the standard test for microbial diagnosis, with directed serological testing (i.e., Q fever serology, Bartonella serology) in culture-negative cases.

choiceRationales.A: An electrocardiogram is a valuable diagnostic tool, but it is not considered strongly suggestive of endocarditis. ECG is useful for assessing the electrical activity of the heart and identifying abnormalities such as arrhythmias or conduction disturbances. However, the definitive diagnosis of endocarditis typically requires other diagnostic procedures.
choiceRationales.B: A chest X-ray is not considered a specific diagnostic test for endocarditis. While it may reveal certain complications or findings associated with endocarditis, such as congestive heart failure or pulmonary infiltrates, it is not a primary tool for confirming the diagnosis of endocarditis.
choiceRationales.C: An echocardiogram, particularly a transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE), is strongly suggestive of endocarditis. Echocardiography allows visualization of heart valves, detection of vegetations, assessment of valvular function, and identification of complications such as abscess formation or valve perforation. TEE is more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) for detecting valvular lesions and is a key diagnostic procedure for endocarditis.
choiceRationales.D: Infective endocarditis is life-threatening; identification of the underlying etiology informs optimized individual patient management. Changing epidemiology, advances in blood culture techniques, and new diagnostics guide the application of laboratory testing for diagnosis of endocarditis. Blood cultures remain the standard test for microbial diagnosis, with directed serological testing (i.e., Q fever serology, Bartonella serology) in culture-negative cases.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: Which part of a long bone is the primary focus of staphylococcal osteomyelitis?
review.explanation: A single pathogenic organism is almost always recovered from the bone in hematogenous osteomyelitis. In adults, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism isolated. Osteomyelitis may be caused from hematogenous spread, direct inoculation of microorganisms into bone, or from a contiguous focus of infection. Hematogenous osteomyelitis usually involves the metaphysis of long bones in children or the vertebral bodies in adults. With hematogenous osteomyelitis, the joint is usually spared from infection in children, unless the metaphysis is intracapsular, as is found at the proximal radius, humerus, or femur.

choiceRationales.A: The epiphyseal line is not the primary focus of staphylococcal osteomyelitis. The epiphyseal line represents the growth plate, and osteomyelitis typically occurs in regions away from the growth plate.
choiceRationales.B: The diaphysis, or the shaft of a long bone, is not the primary focus of staphylococcal osteomyelitis. Osteomyelitis tends to involve areas closer to the metaphysis rather than the diaphysis.
choiceRationales.C: The epiphysis is not the primary focus of staphylococcal osteomyelitis. The epiphysis represents the end part of a long bone, and osteomyelitis typically occurs in regions away from the epiphysis.
choiceRationales.D: A single pathogenic organism is almost always recovered from the bone in hematogenous osteomyelitis. In adults, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism isolated. Osteomyelitis may be caused from hematogenous spread, direct inoculation of microorganisms into bone, or from a contiguous focus of infection. Hematogenous osteomyelitis usually involves the metaphysis of long bones in children or the vertebral bodies in adults. review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: Which of the following will least likely differentiate Taenia saginata from Taenia solium?
review.explanation: Gross morphology of eggs is not a differentiating factor between Taenia saginata and Taenia solium. The eggs of these two species are morphologically indistinguishable. Microscopic examination, as well as consideration of other features like the number of uterine branches and appearance of the scolex, is necessary for accurate identification.

choiceRationales.A: The presence of hooks is a distinguishing factor between T. solium and T. saginata. The scolex of T. solium has 4 suckers with a double row of hooks, while T. saginata has 4 suckers without hooks.
choiceRationales.B: The number of uterine branches is a reliable characteristic for differentiating Taenia saginata from Taenia solium. T. saginata typically has a greater number of uterine branches (14-35) compared to T. solium, which usually has fewer branches (7-20). This difference is a key feature in the morphological identification of these tapeworms.
choiceRationales.C: The appearance of the scolex is a distinguishing feature between Taenia saginata and Taenia solium. The scolex is the anterior end of the tapeworm, and in T. saginata, it is characterized by four strong suckers and lacks hooks. In contrast, T. solium has a scolex with four suckers and a circular double-row of hooks.
choiceRationales.D: Gross morphology of eggs is not a differentiating factor between Taenia saginata and Taenia solium. The eggs of these two species are morphologically indistinguishable. Microscopic examination, as well as consideration of other features like the number of uterine branches and appearance of the scolex, is necessary for accurate identification.

review.stem: Which of the following statements most likely describes heat-stable toxin of E.coli?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

review.explanation: ETEC, a very diverse group of pathogenic E. coli, colonize the small intestine and produce the toxic agents heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxin. Upon ingestion and after reaching the gastrointestinal tract, ETEC colonize the small intestine through an interaction of fimbrial and non-fimbrial adhesins with specific receptors present in the apical membrane of the small intestinal epithelium. choiceRationales.B: This statement is not applicable to the heat-stable toxin of E. coli. STa's main action is within the intestinal cells, influencing ion transport and causing diarrhea. It does not target blood vessels.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is correct. Heat-stable toxin (ST) of E. coli has two classes: STa and STb. However, in the context of human disease, STa is the relevant class, while STb primarily affects swine.

review.stem: Situation 1 - An illness characterized by high grade fever, diffuse red rash that later desquamated, abdominal cramps and diarrhea, shock, and multi-organ failure was reported among women who used tampon during their menstrual period. This was termed as Toxic Shock Syndrome.
review.explanation: Epidemiologic investigation demonstrated that TSS cases were highly associated with the use of absorbent tampons. Subsequent studies established the role of TSST-1 in these illnesses. Most S aureus strains isolated from patients with toxic shock syndrome produce a toxin called toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), which is the same as enterotoxin F. TSST-1 is the prototypical superantigen.

TSST-1 is the prototypical superantigen.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: Situation 3 - A 28 year old full term pregnant delivered her baby while she is having at the same time painful grouped vesicles located on the left mucosal side of her vaginal wall.
review.explanation:
Genital herpes is characterized by vesiculoulcerative lesions of the penis of the male or of the cervix, vulva, vagina, and perineum of the female. The lesions are very painful and may be associated with fever, malaise, dysuria, and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
HSV infection of the newborn may be acquired in utero, during birth, or after birth. The mother is the most common source of infection in all cases. Neonatal herpes is estimated to occur in about 1 in 5000 deliveries per year. The newborn infant seems to be unable to limit the replication and spread of HSV and has a propensity to develop severe disease.
The most common route of infection (~75% of cases) is for HSV to be transmitted to a newborn during birth by contact with herpetic lesions in the birth canal.

choiceRationales.A:
Genital herpes is characterized by vesiculoulcerative lesions of the penis of the male or of the cervix, vulva, vagina, and perineum of the female. The lesions are very painful and may be associated with fever, malaise, dysuria, and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
HSV infection of the newborn may be acquired in utero, during birth, or after birth. The mother is the most common source of infection in all cases. Neonatal herpes is estimated to occur in about 1 in 5000 deliveries per year. The newborn infant seems to be unable to limit the replication and spread of HSV and has a propensity to develop severe disease.

Past medical records prior to her admission showed no abnormal heart findings. She underwent appendectomy one week before the onset of fever. review.explanation: The enterococci have the group D group-specific substance and were previously classified as group D streptococci. Because the group D cell wall–specific antigen is a teichoic acid, it is not an antigenically good marker; enterococci are usually identified by characteristics other than immunologic reactions with group-specific antisera. They are part of the normal enteric microbiota. They are usually nonhemolytic but are occasionally α-hemolytic or rarely β-hemolytic. Enterococci are PYR positive. They grow in the presence of bile, hydrolyze esculin (bile esculin positive) and in contrast to non-enterococcal group D streptococci, they grow well in 6.5% NaCl. Whereas enterococci grow well at between 10 and 45°C, streptococci generally grow at a much narrower temperature range. They are more resistant to penicillin G than the streptococci. Many isolates are vancomycin resistant.

choiceRationales.A: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulase-negative staphylococcus and is a common inhabitant of the skin and mucous membranes. It is a frequent cause of infections related to indwelling medical devices. However, it is not typically associated with causing endocarditis.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: Which of the following statements regarding acute/subacute bacterial endocarditis is TRUE?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has the same pathogenesis as the rheumatic fever

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prompt treatment with high dose penicillin aborts its development

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibiotic susceptibility test are useful for optimal treatment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its more common causative agents are not members of normal microbiota

review.explanation: This statement is true. Antibiotic susceptibility testing helps identify the most effective antibiotics for treating bacterial endocarditis. Since different bacteria may exhibit varying levels of susceptibility to antibiotics, performing susceptibility tests allows healthcare providers to select the most appropriate antibiotic regimen tailored to the specific infecting organism.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is false. Acute/subacute bacterial endocarditis and rheumatic fever have distinct pathogeneses. Acute/subacute bacterial endocarditis is primarily caused by bacterial infection of the heart valves, often by organisms from the normal microbiota, while rheumatic fever is an inflammatory condition that can result from inadequately treated streptococcal throat infections, particularly those caused by Streptococcus pyogenes.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is false. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is crucial in bacterial endocarditis, but it may not necessarily "abort" its development. The damage to heart valves and other complications may already be in progress. Early and appropriate antibiotic therapy is vital for controlling the infection and preventing further complications.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is true. Antibiotic susceptibility testing helps identify the most effective antibiotics for treating bacterial endocarditis. Since different bacteria may exhibit varying levels of susceptibility to antibiotics, performing susceptibility tests allows healthcare providers to select the most appropriate antibiotic regimen tailored to the specific infecting organism.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is false. The more common causative agents of subacute bacterial endocarditis are often members of the normal microbiota, such as viridans streptococci and enterococci. These bacteria can enter the bloodstream from the respiratory or gastrointestinal tract and cause infection in individuals with predisposing conditions, such as abnormal heart valves.

review.stem: Situation 5: HIV is a serious health problem because of the subsequent AIDS.
review.explanation: All primate lentiviruses use as a receptor the CD4 molecule, which is expressed on macrophages and T lymphocytes. A second coreceptor in addition to CD4 is necessary for HIV-1 to gain entry to cells. The second receptor is required for fusion of the virus with the cell membrane. The virus first binds to CD4 and then to the coreceptor. These interactions cause conformational changes in the viral envelope, activating the gp41 fusion peptide and triggering membrane fusion. Chemokine receptors serve as HIV-1 second receptors. (Chemokines are soluble factors with chemoattractant and cytokine properties.) CCR5, the receptor for chemokines RANTES, MIP-1α, and MIP-1β, is the predominant coreceptor for macrophage-tropic strains of HIV-1, whereas CXCR4, the receptor for chemokine SDF-1, is the coreceptor for lymphocyte-tropic strains of HIV-1. The chemokine receptors used by HIV for cell entry are found on lymphocytes, macrophages, and thymocytes as well as on neurons and cells in the colon and cervix. Individuals who possess homozygous deletions in CCR5 or produce mutant forms of the protein may be protected from infection by HIV-1; mutations in the CCR5 gene promoter appear to delay disease progression. The requirement for a coreceptor for HIV fusion with cells provided new targets for antiviral therapeutic strategies, with the first HIV entry inhibitor licensed in the United States in 2003.

choiceRationales.A: CCR5 is a chemokine receptor that serves as a co-receptor for HIV-1 entry into host cells. It is the predominant co-receptor for macrophage-tropic strains of HIV-1. Individuals with homozygous deletions in CCR5 or those producing mutant forms of the protein may exhibit resistance to HIV-1 infection.
choiceRationales.B: There is no known association between HIV entry and CDR24. The primary receptor for HIV is CD4, and chemokine receptors such as CCR5 and CXCR4 act as co-receptors.

Individuals who possess homozygous deletions in CCR5 or produce mutant forms of the protein may be protected from infection by HIV-1; mutations in the CCR5 gene promoter appear to delay disease progression. The requirement for a coreceptor for HIV fusion with cells provided new targets for antiviral therapeutic strategies, with the first HIV entry inhibitor licensed in the United States in 2003.
choiceRationales.D: CXCR4 is another chemokine receptor that acts as a co-receptor for HIV-1 entry into host cells. It is the co-receptor for lymphocyte-tropic strains of HIV-1. The interaction between HIV and CXCR4 is part of the viral entry process.

review.stem: Situation 12 - A 35-year-old female consulted the clinic because of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. The discharge was whitish-gray in color, adherent to the vaginal wall, but none of the cervical os. A wet mount of the vaginal fluid was done. It showed no PMNs, (+) for clue cells with adherent bacilli. Discharge had a fishy odor. What is the MOST PLAUSIBLE clinical diagnosis?
review.explanation:
Bacterial vaginosis is the most prevalent cause of symptomatic vaginitis. The vaginal discharge associated with bacterial vaginosis is thin and gray-white. Speculum examination reveals that the discharge is mildly adherent to the vaginal walls, in contrast to a physiologic discharge, which is in the most dependent areas of the vagina. In women with bacterial vaginosis, the most frequent symptom is an unpleasant vaginal odor, which patients describe as musty or fishy.
The four criteria for the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis are:
A homogeneous vaginal discharge is present.
The vaginal discharge has a pH of 4.5 or higher.
The vaginal discharge has an amine-like odor when mixed with potassium hydroxide, the whiff test.
A wet smear of the vaginal discharge demonstrates clue cells more than 20% of the number of the vaginal epithelial cells.
The classic discharge of Trichomonas infection is termed frothy (with bubbles) and often has an unpleasant odor.
Fungal vaginitis usually presents as a vulvovaginitis. Pruritus is the predominant symptom. The vaginal discharge is white or whitish gray, highly viscous, and described as granular or floccular, with no odor.

choiceRationales.A:

choiceRationales.B: The classic discharge in Trichomonas infection is frothy and may have an unpleasant odor. While Trichomonas infection can cause a fishy odor, the wet smear in this situation showed clue cells, which is more indicative of BV.
choiceRationales.C: Normal ovulatory discharge tends to be clear or white and is not typically associated with a foul odor. In the given scenario, the presence of a fishy odor and clue cells points more towards BV rather than normal ovulation discharge.
choiceRationales.D: Candida infections usually present with a white, curd-like discharge and are often associated with intense pruritus (itching). In this case, the clinical presentation and wet smear findings are more consistent with BV.

review.explanation: Bacterial vaginosis reflects a shift in vaginal flora from lactobacilli-dominant to mixed flora, including genital mycoplasmas, G. vaginalis, and anaerobes, such as peptostreptococci, and Prevotella and Mobiluncus spp. Although Gardnerella and anaerobic organisms can be found in women with normal vaginal flora, their concentration increased several fold in women with bacterial vaginosis concurrent with a marked decrease in lactobacilli.

choiceRationales.B: Poor vaginal hygiene alone is not a direct cause of bacterial vaginosis. BV is more associated with changes in the vaginal microbiota, including a decrease in lactobacilli and an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria.
choiceRationales.C: This description is characteristic of Candida vulvovaginitis, not bacterial vaginosis. Candida infections often present with a white, curd-like discharge.

review.stem: Situation 16 – Escherichia coli is a member of the normal intestinal microbiota. However, certain strains cause diarrheal disease which are extremely common worldwide. Which of the following causes intense and prolonged hypersecretion of water and chlorides and inhibition of the reabsorption of sodium, with ensuing hypermotility and diarrhea lasting for days, similar to Vibrio cholera?
review.explanation: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) are a common cause of "traveler's diarrhea" and a very important cause of diarrhea in children less than 5 years of age in developing countries. This markedly increases the local concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) after which ensues a complex cascade that involves the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. The end result is an intense and prolonged hypersecretion of water and chlorides and inhibition of the reabsorption of sodium. The gut lumen is distended with fluid, and hypermotility and diarrhea ensue, lasting for several days.

choiceRationales.A: STEC, also known as E. coli O157:H7, produces Shiga toxins. These toxins can cause bloody diarrhea and, in severe cases, lead to hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS). However, the mechanism involves damage to the vascular endothelium rather than hypersecretion of water and chlorides.
choiceRationales.B: EIEC invades the intestinal mucosa, causing inflammatory diarrhea with fever and abdominal pain. It does not primarily cause hypersecretion of water and chlorides similar to Vibrio cholera.
choiceRationales.C: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) are a common cause of "traveler's diarrhea" and a very important cause of diarrhea in children less than 5 years of age in developing countries. This markedly increases the local concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) after which ensues a complex cascade that involves the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. The end result is an intense and prolonged hypersecretion of water and chlorides and inhibition of the reabsorption of sodium. The gut lumen is distended with fluid, and hypermotility and diarrhea ensue, lasting for several days.
choiceRationales.D: EPEC attaches to intestinal cells and causes attaching and effacing lesions. It primarily affects the microvilli of enterocytes and is associated with infantile diarrhea. However, it does not cause the same mechanism of hypersecretion as Vibrio cholera.

review.stem: Situation 17 – For the past few days, a 35-year old lady had dry cough associated with low-grade afternoon fever. Physical examinations revealed an emaciated patient with harsh breath sounds on auscultation of the lungs. No enlarged lymph node was observed or palpated. X-ray showed increased density of both upper lung fields.
review.explanation:
Post-primary (Adult-Type) Disease Also referred to as reactivation or secondary TB, post-primary TB is probably most accurately termed adult-type TB because it may result from endogenous reactivation of distant LTBI or recent infection (primary infection or reinfection). It is usually localized to the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, where the substantially higher mean oxygen tension (compared with that in the lower zones) favors mycobacterial growth. The superior segments of the lower lobes are also more frequently involved.
Early in the course of disease, symptoms and signs are often nonspecific and insidious, consisting mainly of diurnal fever and night sweats due to defervescence, weight loss, anorexia, general malaise, and weakness. However, in up to 90% of cases, cough eventually develops—often initially nonproductive and limited to the morning and subsequently accompanied by the production of purulent sputum, sometimes with blood streaking.

choiceRationales.A: The Ghon complex refers to a combination of a primary focus of infection (usually in the lung) and the associated lymph node involvement. It is typically seen in primary tuberculosis. The primary complex consists of a Ghon focus, which is a small subpleural granuloma in the lung, and a Ghon lymph node, which is a corresponding involved regional lymph node. This complex is a characteristic response to the initial infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
choiceRationales.B: Latent tuberculosis (LTBI) refers to a state where an individual is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis but does not currently have active tuberculosis disease. There are no symptoms, and the infection is not contagious. LTBI can progress to active tuberculosis in some individuals, especially if their immune system becomes compromised.
choiceRationales.C:
Post-primary (Adult-Type) Disease Also referred to as reactivation or secondary TB, post-primary TB is probably most accurately termed adult-type TB because it may result from endogenous reactivation of distant LTBI or recent infection (primary infection or reinfection). It is usually localized to the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes, where the substantially higher mean oxygen tension (compared with that in the lower zones) favors mycobacterial growth. The superior segments of the lower lobes are also more frequently involved.
Early in the course of disease, symptoms and signs are often nonspecific and insidious, consisting mainly of diurnal fever and night sweats due to defervescence, weight loss, anorexia, general malaise, and weakness. However, in up to 90% of cases, cough eventually develops—often initially nonproductive and limited to the morning and subsequently accompanied by the production of purulent sputum, sometimes with blood streaking.
choiceRationales.D: Primary tuberculosis occurs upon initial infection with M. tuberculosis. It is characterized by the formation of the Ghon complex, which includes a primary lung focus and associated lymph node involvement. Primary tuberculosis can be asymptomatic or present with mild respiratory symptoms.

review.subject: microbiology
review.stem: What does a positive tuberculin test imply?
review.explanation: A positive tuberculin test result indicates that an individual has been infected in the past. It does not imply that active disease or immunity to disease is present. Tuberculin-positive persons are at risk of developing disease from reactivation of the primary infection, but tuberculin-negative persons who have never been infected are not subject to that risk, although they may become infected from an external source.

choiceRationales.A: A positive tuberculin test result indicates that an individual has been infected in the past. It does not imply that active disease or immunity to disease is present. Tuberculin-positive persons are at risk of developing disease from reactivation of the primary infection, but tuberculin-negative persons who have never been infected are not subject to that risk, although they may become infected from an external source.
choiceRationales.B: A positive tuberculin test alone does not confirm active disease. Additional diagnostic evaluations, such as chest X-rays, sputum cultures, and clinical assessments, are necessary to determine whether the infection is in an active state. Active disease is characterized by the presence of clinical symptoms and signs, as well as radiographic evidence of disease.
choiceRationales.C: A positive tuberculin test does not necessarily indicate immunity to the disease. While the immune response may control the infection and prevent active disease in some individuals, others may develop active tuberculosis if their immune system becomes compromised. Immunity to tuberculosis is complex, and a positive tuberculin test primarily signifies exposure to the bacterium.
choiceRationales.D: A negative tuberculin test may suggest the absence of a previous infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. However, it does not guarantee protection from future infections or rule out the possibility of recent infection.

review.stem: Situation 20 - A 60 yrs old was admitted because of sudden onset of bloody diarrhea associated with lower abdominal pain during each bowel movement. She also exhibited sensorial disturbances and involuntary movement of the upper extremities. Stool examination showed gram-negative bacilli with white blood cells and a few red blood cells. Patient responded to IV fluids and parenteral antibiotics.
review.explanation: Shigellosis is characterized by abdominal cramps, diarrhea, fever, and bloody stools. The clinical signs and symptoms of the disease appear 1 to 3 days after the bacteria are ingested. Shigellae initially colonize the small intestine and begin to multiply within the first 12 hours. The first sign of infection (profuse watery diarrhea without histologic evidence of mucosal invasion) is mediated by an enterotoxin. However, the cardinal feature of shigellosis is lower abdominal cramps and tenesmus (straining to defecate), with abundant pus and blood in the stool. It results from invasion of the colonic mucosa by the bacteria. Abundant neutrophils, erythrocytes, and mucus are found in the stool. Rare but severe symptoms include delirium, encephalopathy, anuria, seizures, meningismus, and coma. The mainstay of treatment of shigellosis is medical management and includes hydration and electrolyte management. Oral rehydration might be adequate in many cases. Fluoroquinolone is recommended for patients with no risk factors for resistance while a third-generation cephalosporin is recommended in high-risk patients. Second-generation cephalosporin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also be used for the treatment of Shigella infection if susceptibility is documented. In pediatrics, the first-line drug is azithromycin if antibiotic susceptibility is unknown.

choiceRationales.A: Escherichia coli is a diverse bacterium, and while some strains can cause gastroenteritis, they typically do not present with the severe symptoms described in the patient's case, such as sensorial disturbances and involuntary movements of the upper extremities. E. coli strains causing gastroenteritis are often associated with watery diarrhea rather than bloody diarrhea.
choiceRationales.B: Shigellosis is characterized by abdominal cramps, diarrhea, fever, and bloody stools. The clinical signs and symptoms of the disease appear 1 to 3 days after the bacteria are ingested. Shigellae initially colonize the small intestine and begin to multiply within the first 12 hours. The first sign of infection (profuse watery diarrhea without histologic evidence of mucosal invasion) is mediated by an enterotoxin. However, the cardinal feature of shigellosis is lower abdominal cramps and tenesmus (straining to defecate), with abundant pus and blood in the stool. It results from invasion of the colonic mucosa by the bacteria. Abundant neutrophils, erythrocytes, and mucus are found in the stool. Rare but severe symptoms include delirium, encephalopathy, anuria, seizures, meningismus, and coma. The mainstay of treatment of shigellosis is medical management and includes hydration and electrolyte management. Oral rehydration might be adequate in many cases. Fluoroquinolone is recommended for patients with no risk factors for resistance while a third-generation cephalosporin is recommended in high-risk patients. Second-generation cephalosporin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can also be used for the treatment of Shigella infection if susceptibility is documented. In pediatrics, the first-line drug is azithromycin if antibiotic susceptibility is unknown.
choiceRationales.C: Salmonella typhi is associated with typhoid fever rather than the symptoms described in the case. Typhoid fever presents with sustained fever, abdominal pain, and other systemic symptoms. Bloody diarrhea is not a typical manifestation of Salmonella typhi infection.
choiceRationales.D: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not a common cause of bacterial dysentery. It is more frequently associated with opportunistic infections in immunocompromised individuals or those with underlying health conditions. The clinical presentation described is not typical for Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.

review.stem: Situation 21 - Janette, a 35 years old sales lady, developed sudden high grade fever, chills, and sharp pleural pain. She also had rusty colored sputum which on gram stain showed gram (+) diplococci, lancet-shaped and arranged in chains. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
review.explanation:
Streptococcus gram-positive cocci typically arranged in pairs or chains (in contrast to the clusters formed by Staphylococcus). Most species are facultative anaerobes, and some grow only in an atmosphere enhanced with carbon dioxide (capnophilic growth).
Carbohydrates are fermented, resulting in the production of lactic acid is catalase negative.
Pneumococcal pneumonia is a type of bacterial pneumonia that is caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (which is also called pneumococcus). The pneumococcus does not have Lancefield Antigens. Under the microscope, they appear as lancet-shaped gram-positive cocci arranged in pairs (diplococci). The major virulence factor of the pneumococcus is its polysaccharide capsule, which protects the organism from phagocytosis.
The onset of the clinical manifestations of pneumococcal pneumonia is abrupt, consisting of a severe shaking chill and sustained fever of 39°C to 41°C. The patient often has symptoms of a viral respiratory tract infection 1 to 3 days before the onset. Most patients have a productive cough with blood-tinged sputum, and they commonly have chest pain (pleurisy). Because the disease is associated with aspiration, it is generally localized in the lower lobes of the lungs (hence the name lobar pneumonia).

review.stem: What is the antibiotic choice for this case?
review.explanation: Treatment of Legionella pneumonia involves antibiotics that target intracellular pathogens, whereas patients with Pontiac fever do not require antibiotic therapy. Macrolides and fluoroquinolones are the first-line agents for Legionella pneumonia according to guidelines in the United States and Europe. Macrolides disrupt protein production critical for survival of the organism. Although erythromycin or clarithromycin is effective, azithromycin is the preferred agent, as it is easier to tolerate and is involved in fewer drug-drug interactions. Azithromycin and clarithromycin also reach higher intracellular concentrations than erythromycin.

choiceRationales.A: Legionella pneumophila produces beta-lactamases, which can inactivate cephalosporins and penicillins. Therefore, penicillin is not the drug of choice.
choiceRationales.B: Treatment of Legionella pneumonia involves antibiotics that target intracellular pathogens, whereas patients with Pontiac fever do not require antibiotic therapy. Macrolides and fluoroquinolones are the first-line agents for Legionella pneumonia according to guidelines in the United States and Europe. Macrolides disrupt protein production critical for survival of the organism. Although erythromycin or clarithromycin is effective, azithromycin is the preferred agent, as it is easier to tolerate and is involved in fewer drug-drug interactions. Azithromycin and clarithromycin also reach higher intracellular concentrations than erythromycin.
choiceRationales.C:
Fluoroquinolones, such as levofloxacin, are also effective against Legionella pneumophila. They are considered an alternative option for treatment. However, the case involves a 60 year old patient, fluoroquinolones have been associated with tendon rupture in this age-group hence, it is not the best drug of choice.
Fluoroquinolones are potent agents against Legionella species. Data from both in vitro and in vivo models of infection suggest that fluoroquinolones may be more effective than macrolides, but no randomized clinical trials have yet compared the two drug classes for treatment of legionellosis. In nonrandomized observational studies, fluoroquinolones have been shown to be more effective than macrolides (erythromycin and clarithromycin) in terms of fever resolution and decreased duration of hospitalization; other such studies have shown no difference in outcome.
choiceRationales.D: Tetracyclines, including doxycycline, are another class of antibiotics effective against Legionella pneumophila. They are often used as an alternative or in combination therapy.

review.stem: Situation 24 - antibiotic resistance is a growing concern in the treatment of infection. Resistance to nafcillin, and to methicillin and oxacillin (MRSA) is the more commonly known example of this problem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alteration in the bacterial cell wall

review.explanation: Microorganisms produce enzymes that destroy the active drug. Examples: Staphylococci resistant to penicillin G produce a β-lactamase that destroys the drug. Other β-lactamases are produced by gram-negative rods. Gram-negative bacteria resistant to aminoglycosides (by virtue of a plasmid) produce adenylating, phosphorylating, or acetylating enzymes that destroy the drug.

choiceRationales.A: Plasmids are extrachromosomal genetic elements that can carry genes encoding resistance to antibiotics. Bacteria can transfer plasmids containing resistance genes to each other, promoting the spread of antibiotic resistance.
choiceRationales.B: Microorganisms produce enzymes that destroy the active drug. Examples: Staphylococci resistant to penicillin G produce a β-lactamase that destroys the drug. choiceRationales.C: SCCmec is a mobile genetic element found in Staphylococcus aureus, particularly in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). It carries the mecA gene, which encodes penicillin-binding protein 2a (PBP2a), a key factor in methicillin resistance.
choiceRationales.D: Some bacteria can develop resistance by altering components of their cell wall that are targeted by antibiotics. This can involve changes in the structure of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), which are involved in cell wall synthesis.

review.stem: What is the plausible reason for therapeutic failure with Penicillin, et. Al., and success with Tetracycline et. Al.?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Plasmin mediated resistance to penicillin et. al.

review.explanation:
This is correct in the case of Mycoplasma pneumonia, but the primary reason for the therapeutic failure with penicillin is the lack of a cell wall, not a defective one.
Mycoplasma pneumonia lacks a cell wall, making it inherently resistant to antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis, such as penicillin and other beta-lactam antibiotics.
Beta-lactam antibiotics like penicillin work by inhibiting cell wall synthesis, and their efficacy depends on the presence of a cell wall in bacteria.
Mycoplasma pneumonia has a unique cell membrane structure and does not possess a cell wall, rendering it insensitive to beta-lactam antibiotics.
Tetracycline and erythromycin, which target bacterial protein synthesis and are effective against organisms lacking cell walls, are suitable alternatives for treating Mycoplasma pneumonia.

choiceRationales.A: Plasmin is not typically associated with resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics.
choiceRationales.B: Mycoplasma pneumoniae does not produce beta-lactamases because it does not have a cell wall. The lack of a cell wall in Mycoplasma pneumonia makes it inherently resistant to penicillin and related antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis. Tetracyclines, with their distinct mechanism of action targeting protein synthesis, are effective against Mycoplasma pneumonia.
choiceRationales.C:
This is correct in the case of Mycoplasma pneumonia, but the primary reason for the therapeutic failure with penicillin is the lack of a cell wall, not a defective one.

Tetracycline and erythromycin, which target bacterial protein synthesis and are effective against organisms lacking cell walls, are suitable alternatives for treating Mycoplasma pneumonia.
choiceRationales.D:
Tetracyclines are a type of broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotics that work by inhibiting protein synthesis. They are able to enter microorganisms through both passive diffusion and an energy-dependent process of active transport. Once inside the cell, tetracyclines bind reversibly to the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome, preventing the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the acceptor site on the mRNA-ribosome complex. This effectively stops the addition of amino acids to the growing peptide.
These antibiotics are effective against a wide range of bacteria, including many gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, certain anaerobes, rickettsiae, chlamydiae, and mycoplasmas. While most tetracyclines have similar antibacterial activities, some tetracycline-resistant strains may still be susceptible to certain tetracycline analogs like doxycycline, minocycline, and tigecycline. These analogs are poor substrates for the efflux pump, which may be the mechanism of resistance. Minor differences in clinical efficacy for susceptible organisms can be attributed largely to the absorption, distribution, and excretion of individual drugs.
There are three main mechanisms of resistance to tetracycline analogs: impaired influx or increased efflux by an active transport protein pump, ribosome protection due to the production of proteins that interfere with tetracycline binding to the ribosome, and enzymatic inactivation. The most significant of these are the production of an efflux pump and ribosomal protection.

review.stem: Situation 28- Eight hours after eating in a fiesta, Anna developed nausea and vomiting, headache, profuse diarrhea and low grade fever. Blood culture was negative for growth but the stool culture was positive. Repeated blood culture remained negative while stool culture was positive even 2 weeks after the initial examination. What was the MOST PROBABLE “growth” in the stool culture?
review.explanation:
Enterocolitis is the most prevalent manifestation of salmonella infection. In the United States, prominent causative agents of enterocolitis include S. typhimurium and Salmonella Enteritidis, although any of the more than 1400 group 1 serotypes of salmonellae can also cause this condition. Following the ingestion of salmonellae, symptoms typically appear within 8-48 hours, including nausea, headache, vomiting, and profuse diarrhea with few leukocytes in the stools. Low-grade fever is common, but the episode usually resolves in 2-3 days.
Inflammatory lesions of the small and large intestine are typically present. Bacteremia is rare, occurring in only 2-4% of cases, except in immunodeficient individuals. Blood culture results are usually negative, but stool culture results are positive for salmonellae and may remain positive for several weeks after clinical recovery.

choiceRationales.A:
Salmonella cholerasuis can cause gastroenteritis characterized by symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, headache, profuse diarrhea, and low-grade fever.

review.explanation: This is the correct and often preferred management for Stage IIIB cervical cancer. In such cases, surgery alone is often not the preferred treatment because the disease has advanced beyond what surgery can effectively address.
choiceRationales.B: Cervical conization involves the removal of a cone-shaped piece of tissue from the cervix. While this procedure may be suitable for certain early-stage cervical cancers, it is not typically recommended for Stage IIIB cervical cancer, where the disease has spread extensively.

choiceRationales.D: Radical trachelectomy is a surgical option that involves the removal of the cervix and surrounding tissues while preserving the uterus. review.stem: Fetal risk factors of a diabetic pregnant woman includes the following, EXCEPT:
review.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy. While it is not directly associated with diabetes, it can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, which may have indirect effects on fetal well-being. Proper management of hyperemesis is essential to minimize its impact.

choiceRationales.A: Sudden fetal death, or stillbirth, can be a concern in pregnancies complicated by diabetes. Poorly controlled diabetes, especially if there are fluctuations in blood glucose levels, can increase the risk of stillbirth. Strict glycemic control and regular monitoring are crucial to reduce this risk.
choiceRationales.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting during pregnancy. While it is not directly associated with diabetes, it can lead to dehydration and electrolyte imbalances, which may have indirect effects on fetal well-being. Proper management of hyperemesis is essential to minimize its impact.
choiceRationales.C: Miscarriage, or spontaneous abortion, may occur in pregnancies complicated by diabetes. Poorly controlled diabetes, particularly in the early stages of pregnancy, can increase the risk of miscarriage. Good glycemic control is crucial to reduce this risk.
choiceRationales.D: Polyhydramnios, an excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid, is a potential complication of diabetes during pregnancy. It can result from fetal hyperglycemia, leading to increased urine production by the fetus. Polyhydramnios is associated with an increased risk of preterm labor and delivery.

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: A 40/F comes to you complaining of easy fatigability. On PE, she is pale and slightly tachycardic. On a CBC, she has a low hemoglobin, low MCV and normal reticulocyte count. Which of the following is the likely cause of her anemia?
review.explanation:
Signs related to iron deficiency depend on the severity and chronicity of the anemia in addition to the usual signs of anemia—fatigue, pallor, and reduced exercise capacity. Cheilosis (fissures at the corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails) are signs of advanced tissue iron deficiency.
Careful evaluation of the peripheral blood smear reveals the first appearance of microcytic cells, and if the laboratory technology is available, one finds hypochromic reticulocytes in circulation. Gradually, the hemoglobin and hematocrit begin to fall, reflecting iron-deficiency anemia. The transferrin saturation at this point is 10–15%.
When moderate anemia is present (hemoglobin 10–13 g/dL), the bone marrow remains hypoproliferative. With more severe anemia (hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL), hypochromia and microcytosis become more prominent, target cells and misshapen red cells (poikilocytes) appear on the blood smear as cigar- or pencil-shaped forms, and the erythroid marrow becomes increasingly ineffective.

With more severe anemia (hemoglobin 7–8 g/dL), hypochromia and microcytosis become more prominent, target cells and misshapen red cells (poikilocytes) appear on the blood smear as cigar- or pencil-shaped forms, and the erythroid marrow becomes increasingly ineffective.
choiceRationales.B: Vitamin K deficiency is not a common cause of anemia. Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and its deficiency is more likely to result in bleeding disorders rather than anemia.
choiceRationales.C: Folate deficiency leads to macrocytic anemia (increased MCV), not microcytic anemia. Folate is necessary for DNA synthesis and cell division.
choiceRationales.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency also leads to macrocytic anemia (increased MCV). It is essential for DNA synthesis and neurological function.

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: PAS-positive cytoplasmic inclusions known as Bunina bodies are:
review.explanation:
Bunina bodies, which are small eosinophilic intraneuronal inclusions in the remaining lower motor neurons, are generally considered to be a specific pathologic hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
Bunina bodies coexisting with TDP-43-immunoreactive skein-like inclusions (SIs) and round inclusions (RIs) in lower motor neurons are a frequent feature of sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Previous studies have shown that bunina bodies and TDP-43-IR inclusions are often detected in association with autophagy-related structures (autophagosomes and autolysosomes). Ultrastructurally, SIs and mature bunina bodies contain autophagosomes and autolysosomes. Mature bunina bodies are localized in the vicinity of SIs. RIs also contain autophagosomes, autolysosomes, and early-stage BBs. These findings suggest that autophagy is a common degradation pathway for BBs and TDP-43-IR inclusions, which may explain their frequent coexistence.

choiceRationales.A: Alpha-synuclein protein is more commonly associated with conditions like Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia, not ALS.

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: A 25-year old sales lady stepped into the elevator full of people with influenza, coughing and sneezing. The viral particles which she inhaled attached to her respiratory epithelium. Which immune cell is MOST likely to rapidly destroy the virally infected cells?
review.explanation: NK cells are innate immune cells, as they are functional without prior activation and do not express highly variable and clonally distributed receptors for antigens. Instead, NK cells have two types of receptors—inhibitory and activating. Inhibitory receptors recognize self class I MHC molecules, which are expressed on all healthy cells, whereas activating receptors recognize molecules that are expressed or upregulated on stressed or infected cells. Normally, the effects of inhibitory receptors dominate over those of activating receptors, preventing spontaneous activation of the NK cells. Infections (especially viral infections) and stress are associated with reduced expression of class I MHC molecules and increased expression of proteins that engage activating receptors. The net result is that the NK cells are activated and the infected or stressed cells are killed and eliminated.

choiceRationales.A: NK cells are innate immune cells, as they are functional without prior activation and do not express highly variable and clonally distributed receptors for antigens. Instead, NK cells have two types of receptors—inhibitory and activating. Inhibitory receptors recognize self class I MHC molecules, which are expressed on all healthy cells, whereas activating receptors recognize molecules that are expressed or upregulated on stressed or infected cells. Normally, the effects of inhibitory receptors dominate over those of activating receptors, preventing spontaneous activation of the NK cells. Infections (especially viral infections) and stress are associated with reduced expression of class I MHC molecules and increased expression of proteins that engage activating receptors. The net result is that the NK cells are activated and the infected or stressed cells are killed and eliminated.
choiceRationales.B: CD4+ cells, also known as T helper cells, are primarily involved in orchestrating the immune response. They play a crucial role in activating other immune cells, including CD8+ cytotoxic T cells. While CD4+ cells are essential for a coordinated and effective immune response, they do not directly destroy virally infected cells. Instead, they assist in coordinating the overall immune reaction.
choiceRationales.C: Dendritic cells (DCs) are the most important antigen presenting cells for initiating T-cell responses against protein antigens. APCs are specialized to capture antigens and display these to lymphocytes.
choiceRationales.D: Macrophages are derivatives of peripheral blood monocytes are members of the mononuclear phagocyte system of cells. Macrophages secrete a variety of cytokines, including interleukin-1 (Il-1), as well as other products, such as acid hydrolases, neutral proteases, and prostaglandins. In addition, they process and present antigen (along with human leukocyte antigen [HLA] class II antigens) to CD4+ T cells. They also participate in delayed hypersensitivity reactions. They may be capable of directly killing tumor cells.

review.stem: Tita Lydia has been diagnosed to have Congestive Heart Failure for the past 3 years. Upon review of her history, it was noted that she developed productive rust-colored sputum for the past 2 months. Her doctor requested sputum cytology which revealed numerous hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Which subcellular structures found in macrophages explains the accumulation of this pigment?
review.explanation: RBCs that lose their flexibility, presumably due to cumulative membrane damage, are trapped within the spleen and phagocytized by fixed macrophages. During phagocytosis, DMT1 is also internalized by the macrophages. When senescent RBCs are digested, heme is released from globulin, and the globin chains are digested to amino acids. As in enterocytes, macrophage heme oxygenase removes ferrous iron from heme, and the ferrous iron enters into the cytoplasm from the phagolysosome via DMT1. HRG1 (solute carrier family 48 [heme transporter], member 1; 146 amino acids; 16.4 kDa; gene location, chromosome 12q13.11) appears to be able to transport heme directly from the macrophage phagolysosome into the cell cytoplasm. HRG1 may also be functional in enterocytes.

choiceRationales.A: Ribosomes are cellular structures involved in protein synthesis. They are not directly related to the accumulation of hemosiderin in macrophages. Hemosiderin is a complex of iron and protein, and its accumulation is more closely associated with the breakdown of red blood cells and subsequent handling of iron by macrophages.
choiceRationales.B: RBCs that lose their flexibility, presumably due to cumulative membrane damage, are trapped within the spleen and phagocytized by fixed macrophages. During phagocytosis, DMT1 is also internalized by the macrophages. When senescent RBCs are digested, heme is released from globulin, and the globin chains are digested to amino acids. As in enterocytes, macrophage heme oxygenase removes ferrous iron from heme, and the ferrous iron enters into the cytoplasm from the phagolysosome via DMT1. HRG1 (solute carrier family 48 [heme transporter], member 1; 146 amino acids; 16.4 kDa; gene location, chromosome 12q13.11) appears to be able to transport heme directly from the macrophage phagolysosome into the cell cytoplasm. HRG1 may also be functional in enterocytes.
choiceRationales.C: The Golgi apparatus is involved in processing and packaging proteins for secretion. While it plays a role in cellular trafficking and modification of proteins, it is not directly associated with the accumulation of hemosiderin in macrophages.
choiceRationales.D: The endoplasmic reticulum is involved in the synthesis and folding of proteins. It is not directly implicated in the accumulation of hemosiderin in macrophages.
