review.subject: pathology
review.stem: Your grandmother who is 95 years old accidentally touches a pot of boiling water. The skin of her finger in 2 hours then revealed marked erythema and small blisters. This event has led to which inflammatory response?
review.explanation:
Serous inflammation is marked by the exudation of cell-poor fluid into spaces created by cell injury or into body cavities lined by the peritoneum, pleura, or pericardium.
Typically, the fluid in serous inflammation is not infected by destructive organisms and does not contain large numbers of leukocytes (which tend to produce purulent inflammation.
In body cavities, the fluid may be derived from the plasma (as a result of increased vascular permeability) or from the secretions of mesothelial cells (as a result of local irritation); accumulation of fluid in these cavities is called an effusion.
The skin blister resulting from a burn or viral infection represents the accumulation of serous fluid within or immediately beneath the damaged epidermis of the skin.

choiceRationales.A:
Serous inflammation is marked by the exudation of cell-poor fluid into spaces created by cell injury or into body cavities lined by the peritoneum, pleura, or pericardium.
Typically, the fluid in serous inflammation is not infected by destructive organisms and does not contain large numbers of leukocytes (which tend to produce purulent inflammation.
In body cavities, the fluid may be derived from the plasma (as a result of increased vascular permeability) or from the secretions of mesothelial cells (as a result of local irritation); accumulation of fluid in these cavities is called an effusion.
The skin blister resulting from a burn or viral infection represents the accumulation of serous fluid within or immediately beneath the damaged epidermis of the skin.
choiceRationales.B: Purulent inflammation, also known as suppurative inflammation, is characterized by the presence of pus, which consists of neutrophils, debris, and necrotic cells. This type of inflammation typically occurs in response to bacterial infections. The fluid is thick and opaque. Purulent inflammation is often associated with abscess formation.
choiceRationales.C: Granulomatous inflammation is characterized by the formation of granulomas, which are collections of immune cells, particularly macrophages, that form a nodular structure. This type of inflammation is often associated with chronic infections (e.g., tuberculosis), autoimmune diseases (e.g., sarcoidosis), or exposure to certain foreign materials.
choiceRationales.D: Fibrinous inflammation is characterized by the exudation of fibrin-rich fluid. This type of inflammation is often seen in the lining of body cavities during inflammation and can lead to the formation of fibrin deposits. Fibrinous inflammation may occur in response to severe injuries or inflammatory conditions.

A. Serous
B. Purulent
C. Granulomatous
D. Fibrinous

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: Which of the following statements regarding pheochromocytoma is TRUE?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only 10% of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant

choices.label: B
choices.text: A germline mutation is present in all pheochromocytomas

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adrenal pheochromocytomas are always associated with hypertension

review.explanation:
Pheochromocytomas are neoplasms composed of chromaffin cells, which synthesize and release catecholamines and in some instances peptide hormones. It is important to recognize these tumors because they are a rare cause of surgically correctable hypertension. Traditionally, the features of pheochromocytomas have been summarized by the “rule of 10s”.
Ten percent of pheochromocytomas are extra-adrenal, occurring in sites such as the organs of Zuckerkandl and the carotid body. Pheochromocytomas that develop in extra-adrenal paraganglia are designated paragangliomas.
Ten percent of sporadic adrenal pheochromocytomas are bilateral; this figure may rise to as high as 50% in cases that are associated with familial tumor syndromes.
Ten percent of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant, defined by the presence of metastatic disease. Malignancy is more common (20% to 40%) in extra-adrenal paragangliomas, and in tumors arising in the setting of certain germline mutations.
One “traditional” 10% rule that has now been modified pertains to familial cases. It is now recognized that as many as 25% of individuals with pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas harbor a germline mutation in one of at least six known genes.
Ten percent of adrenal pheochromocytomas are not associated with hypertension. Of the 90% that present with hypertension, approximately two thirds have “paroxysmal” episodes associated with sudden rise in blood pressure and palpitations, which can, on occasion, be fatal.

choiceRationales.A:
Pheochromocytomas are neoplasms composed of chromaffin cells, which synthesize and release catecholamines and in some instances peptide hormones. It is important to recognize these tumors because they are a rare cause of surgically correctable hypertension. Traditionally, the features of pheochromocytomas have been summarized by the “rule of 10s”.
Ten percent of pheochromocytomas are extra-adrenal, occurring in sites such as the organs of Zuckerkandl and the carotid body. Pheochromocytomas that develop in extra-adrenal paraganglia are designated paragangliomas.
Ten percent of sporadic adrenal pheochromocytomas are bilateral; this figure may rise to as high as 50% in cases that are associated with familial tumor syndromes.
Ten percent of adrenal pheochromocytomas are biologically malignant, defined by the presence of metastatic disease. Malignancy is more common (20% to 40%) in extra-adrenal paragangliomas, and in tumors arising in the setting of certain germline mutations.
One “traditional” 10% rule that has now been modified pertains to familial cases. It is now recognized that as many as 25% of individuals with pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas harbor a germline mutation in one of at least six known genes.
Ten percent of adrenal pheochromocytomas are not associated with hypertension. Of the 90% that present with hypertension, approximately two thirds have “paroxysmal” episodes associated with sudden rise in blood pressure and palpitations, which can, on occasion, be fatal.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is not true. While it is recognized that a significant portion of individuals with pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas harbor germline mutations (approximately 25%), it is not present in all cases. Germline mutations are associated with hereditary forms of pheochromocytomas, but sporadic cases also exist without a germline mutation.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is not true. While the majority (approximately 90%) of adrenal pheochromocytomas are associated with hypertension, there is a subset (10%) that does not present with hypertension. Additionally, among those with hypertension, approximately two-thirds may experience paroxysmal episodes characterized by a sudden rise in blood pressure and palpitations.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is partially true. Approximately 10% of sporadic adrenal pheochromocytomas are bilateral, but bilaterality is not a definitive marker of malignancy. The risk of malignancy is higher in bilateral cases, particularly in those associated with familial tumor syndromes, but malignancy is determined by the presence of metastatic disease rather than the bilaterality per se.

D. Bilaterality is associated with malignancy

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: What morphological changes will be MOST likely expected to find in a patient with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Preserved volume of the upper neurons along the corticospinal tract

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thinning of the anterior roots of the spinal cord due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertrophic precentral motor gyrus in the cortex to compensate for lower motor neuron loss

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relatively preserved number of anterior horn neurons throughout the length of the spinal cord

review.explanation: The anterior roots of the spinal cord are thin due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers, and the precentral motor gyrus in the cortex may be atrophic in especially severe cases. There is a reduction in the number of anterior-horn neurons throughout the length of the spinal cord, associated with reactive gliosis. Similar findings are seen in the hypoglossal, ambiguus, and motor trigeminal cranial nerve nuclei. Remaining neurons often contain PAS-positive cytoplasmic inclusions called Bunina bodies, which appear to be remnants of autophagic vacuoles. Skeletal muscles innervated by the degenerated lower motor neurons show neurogenic atrophy. Loss of the upper motor neurons leads to degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, resulting in volume loss and absence of myelinated fibers, which may be particularly evident at the lower segmental levels.

choiceRationales.A: In Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), there is degeneration of both upper motor neurons (UMNs) in the cerebral cortex and lower motor neurons (LMNs) in the brainstem and spinal cord. There is no preservation of volume in the corticospinal tract; rather, atrophy and degeneration occur, leading to a loss of motor function.
choiceRationales.B: The anterior roots of the spinal cord are thin due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers, and the precentral motor gyrus in the cortex may be atrophic in especially severe cases. There is a reduction in the number of anterior-horn neurons throughout the length of the spinal cord, associated with reactive gliosis. Similar findings are seen in the hypoglossal, ambiguus, and motor trigeminal cranial nerve nuclei. Remaining neurons often contain PAS-positive cytoplasmic inclusions called Bunina bodies, which appear to be remnants of autophagic vacuoles. Skeletal muscles innervated by the degenerated lower motor neurons show neurogenic atrophy. Loss of the upper motor neurons leads to degeneration of the corticospinal tracts, resulting in volume loss and absence of myelinated fibers, which may be particularly evident at the lower segmental levels.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is not accurate. In ALS, there is no compensatory hypertrophy of the precentral motor gyrus in the cortex. Instead, there is degeneration of the upper motor neurons in the cerebral cortex, contributing to the overall loss of motor function.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is not accurate. ALS is characterized by the progressive degeneration and loss of both upper and lower motor neurons. There is no preservation of the number of anterior horn neurons; instead, there is atrophy and degeneration, leading to motor dysfunction.

A. Preserved volume of the upper neurons along the corticospinal tract
B. Thinning of the anterior roots of the spinal cord due to loss of lower motor neuron fibers
C. Hypertrophic precentral motor gyrus in the cortex to compensate for lower motor neuron loss
D. Relatively preserved number of anterior horn neurons throughout the length of the spinal cord

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: Imaging studies showed a connection from the bladder to the umbilicus in female infant who often wet the top of her diaper. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
review.explanation: This is the most likely diagnosis based on the described symptoms. The urachus is a structure that connects the fetal bladder to the umbilicus during development. Normally, it obliterates, forming the median umbilical ligament. If it fails to close completely, a persistent urachus can result, leading to a communication between the bladder and the umbilicus. This condition is often associated with urinary leakage, and in the described case, the wetting of the top of the diaper could be indicative of urine drainage through the umbilicus.

choiceRationales.A: The vitelline duct, also known as the omphalomesenteric duct, normally connects the developing embryo's midgut to the yolk sac. It usually obliterates during embryonic development. If a remnant persists, it can lead to various anomalies. However, a connection from the bladder to the umbilicus is not typically associated with a vitelline duct remnant.
choiceRationales.B: This is the most likely diagnosis based on the described symptoms. The urachus is a structure that connects the fetal bladder to the umbilicus during development. Normally, it obliterates, forming the median umbilical ligament. If it fails to close completely, a persistent urachus can result, leading to a communication between the bladder and the umbilicus. This condition is often associated with urinary leakage, and in the described case, the wetting of the top of the diaper could be indicative of urine drainage through the umbilicus.
choiceRationales.C: Exstrophy of the bladder is a developmental failure in the anterior wall of the abdomen and the bladder, so that the bladder either communicates directly through a large defect with the surface of the body or lies as an opened sac.
choiceRationales.D: Diverticula are pouchlike evaginations of the bladder wall that vary from less than 1 cm to 5 to 10 cm in diameter and may be congenital or acquired. Congenital diverticula may be due to a focal failure of development of the normal musculature or to some urinary tract obstruction during fetal development. Acquired diverticula are most often seen with prostatic enlargement (hyperplasia or neoplasia), producing obstruction to urine outflow and marked muscle thickening of the bladder wall. The increased intravesical pressure causes outpouching of the bladder wall and the formation of diverticula.

D. Congenital diverticulum

review.stem: Tita Luz, 55 years old, comes to your clinic for undocumented fever, and productive cough with yellowish sputum of 2 days duration. Persistent pertinent findings in her physical examination reveal slight tachypnea and audible crackles at the lung bases. Chest radiographs show patchy infiltrates in both lungs. Which of the following inflammatory cells will MOST likely be seen increased when a sample of respiratory sputum is sent for analysis?
review.explanation: These signs and symptoms suggest acute bacterial pneumonia. Such infections induce an acute inflammation dominated by neutrophils that fill alveoli, and are coughed up, which gives the sputum its yellowish, purulent appearance. Langhans giant cells are seen with granulomatous inflammatory responses. Macrophages become more numerous after initiation of acute events, cleaning up tissue and bacterial debris through phagocytosis. Mast cells are better known as participants in allergic and anaphylactic responses. Lymphocytes are a feature of chronic inflammation.

choiceRationales.A: These signs and symptoms suggest acute bacterial pneumonia. Such infections induce an acute inflammation dominated by neutrophils that fill alveoli, and are coughed up, which gives the sputum its yellowish, purulent appearance. Langhans giant cells are seen with granulomatous inflammatory responses. Macrophages become more numerous after initiation of acute events, cleaning up tissue and bacterial debris through phagocytosis. Mast cells are better known as participants in allergic and anaphylactic responses. Lymphocytes are a feature of chronic inflammation.
choiceRationales.B: While macrophages are also important immune cells, they are more associated with chronic inflammatory processes. In acute bacterial infections like pneumonia, the initial response is often dominated by neutrophils. However, macrophages play a role in the later stages of infection and are involved in clearing cellular debris and promoting tissue repair.
choiceRationales.C: Mast cells are primarily involved in allergic and hypersensitivity reactions. In the context of a bacterial respiratory infection, they are not the predominant inflammatory cells. Their role is more prominent in conditions such as asthma or allergic rhinitis.
choiceRationales.D: T lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell involved in adaptive immunity. They play a crucial role in the immune response but are more associated with viral and chronic infections. In acute bacterial infections, the initial response is typically characterized by neutrophil infiltration.

review.subject: pathology
review.stem: What are these morphologically atypical keratinocytes described as enlarged cells with eccentric, pyknotic nuclei surrounded by a perinuclear halo, found in human papilloma virus infection?
review.explanation: Histopathologically, the hallmark of an HPV-infected cell is the development of morphologically atypical keratinocytes known as koilocytes. These are enlarged cells with eccentric, pyknotic nuclei that are often surrounded by a perinuclear halo. Generally, the epidermis will show a marked acanthosis with varying degrees of papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and parakeratosis as well as a complete effacement of the granular cell layer. Rete ridges tend to be elongated and point inward toward the center of the wart, and the dermis will often display an increased vascularization with the presence of thrombosed capillaries. In morphologically ambiguous lesions, definitive diagnosis can best be made through the use of electron microscopy and the immunohistochemical peroxidase-antiperoxidase stain. These methods will enable the direct visualization of viral particles within the cells. Additionally, the use of MIB1, an antibody targeting cell proliferation protein Ki-67, may also be helpful in highlighting the presence of viral infection.

choiceRationales.A: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies are crystalloid structures found in the cytoplasm of neoplastic cells in malakoplakia, a rare inflammatory condition. These bodies are not associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection.
choiceRationales.B: Schiller-Duval bodies are characteristic structures seen in yolk sac tumors, a type of germ cell tumor. They consist of a central blood vessel surrounded by tumor cells. These structures are not associated with HPV infection.
choiceRationales.C: Acanthosis refers to epidermal hyperplasia, which is an increase in the thickness of the stratum spinosum layer of the epidermis. While acanthosis can be seen in various skin conditions, it is not a specific feature of HPV infection.
choiceRationales.D: Histopathologically, the hallmark of an HPV-infected cell is the development of morphologically atypical keratinocytes known as koilocytes. These are enlarged cells with eccentric, pyknotic nuclei that are often surrounded by a perinuclear halo. Generally, the epidermis will show a marked acanthosis with varying degrees of papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and parakeratosis as well as a complete effacement of the granular cell layer. Rete ridges tend to be elongated and point inward toward the center of the wart, and the dermis will often display an increased vascularization with the presence of thrombosed capillaries. These methods will enable the direct visualization of viral particles within the cells. Additionally, the use of MIB1, an antibody targeting cell proliferation protein Ki-67, may also be helpful in highlighting the presence of viral infection.

review.stem: Once bacteria enter the body, leukocytes leave the vasculature then migrate towards the site of bacterial inoculation. Which of the following substances is MOST likely responsible for the movement of the said leukocytes?
review.explanation:
After exiting the circulation, leukocytes move in the tissues toward the site of injury by a process called chemotaxis, which is defined as locomotion along a chemical gradient. Both exogenous and endogenous substances can act as chemoattractants, including the following:
Bacterial products, particularly peptides with N-formylmethionine termini
Cytokines, especially those of the chemokine family
Components of the complement system, particularly C5a
Products of the lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid (AA) metabolism, particularly leukotriene B4 (LTB4)
These chemoattractants are produced by microbes and by host cells in response to infections and tissue damage and during immunologic reactions. All act by binding to seven transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors on the surface of leukocytes. Signals initiated from these receptors activate second messengers that induce polymerization of actin, resulting in increased amounts at the leading edge of the cell and localization of myosin filaments at the back. The leukocyte moves by extending filopodia that pull the back of the cell in the direction of extension, much like the front wheels pull an automobile with front-wheel drive. The net result is that leukocytes migrate toward the inflammatory stimulus in the direction of the locally produced chemoattractants.

choiceRationales.A: Complement C3a is a component of the complement system, and its activation can contribute to inflammation. However, in the context of leukocyte migration towards the site of bacterial inoculation, the primary role of complement is often attributed to complement products such as C5a. C5a is a potent chemoattractant for leukocytes.
choiceRationales.B: Histamine is released during inflammatory reactions and can increase vascular permeability, leading to the extravasation of leukocytes. While histamine plays a role in the early stages of inflammation, it is not a direct chemotactic factor guiding leukocytes to the site of bacterial inoculation.
choiceRationales.C: Prostaglandins are lipid mediators that play a role in inflammation, but they are not typically involved in the direct chemotaxis of leukocytes. Prostaglandins can contribute to vasodilation and pain sensation.

review.stem: If ACTH is elevated and completely insensitive to low or high doses of dexamethasone, what is the probable cause of Cushing Syndrome?
review.explanation: Ectopic ACTH secretion refers to the production of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) by non-pituitary tumors, often malignant ones, outside the pituitary gland. These tumors can autonomously produce ACTH, leading to increased cortisol production by the adrenal glands. In this context, the elevated ACTH is not subject to the normal feedback inhibition by glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone.

choiceRationales.A: Ectopic ACTH secretion refers to the production of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) by non-pituitary tumors, often malignant ones, outside the pituitary gland. These tumors can autonomously produce ACTH, leading to increased cortisol production by the adrenal glands. In this context, the elevated ACTH is not subject to the normal feedback inhibition by glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone.
choiceRationales.B: An adrenal tumor, specifically an adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, can autonomously produce cortisol. In such cases, the cortisol production is not regulated by ACTH from the pituitary gland. As a result, the ACTH levels is low while the cortisol levels are high. Adrenal tumors are also insensitive to the dexamethasone suppression test.
choiceRationales.C: A pituitary adenoma, specifically one that produces excess ACTH (Cushing's disease), can lead to increased cortisol production by the adrenal glands. However, in Cushing's disease, the pituitary tumor is typically sensitive to dexamethasone suppression. If ACTH remains elevated despite high-dose dexamethasone, it may suggest an ectopic source.
choiceRationales.D: Administration of exogenous glucocorticoids can suppress the release of ACTH by the pituitary gland. However, if Cushing syndrome persists despite high-dose dexamethasone administration, it suggests an autonomous source of cortisol production, such as an adrenal tumor or ectopic ACTH secretion.

review.stem: Glycogen storage diseases come from a hereditary deficiency of one of the enzymes involved in the synthesis or sequential degradation of glycogen. In the hepatic form of this group of diseases, the liver cells store glycogen because of the deficiency of which enzymes?
review.explanation:
The deficiency of Glucose-6-phosphatase is associated with Von Gierke disease, which is the hepatic form of glycogen storage disease. In Von Gierke disease, the liver is unable to convert glycogen into glucose due to the absence of glucose-6-phosphatase. This results in the accumulation of glycogen in the liver, leading to hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia.
In the hepatic form of glycogen storage diseases, the liver cells store glycogen because of the deficiency of d. Glucose-6-phosphatase. This enzyme is crucial for the final step in gluconeogenesis, allowing the release of glucose from glycogen stores in the liver. The absence of glucose-6-phosphatase in Von Gierke disease leads to impaired glycogen breakdown in the liver.

However, Pompe disease primarily affects muscle cells rather than the liver. The deficiency of acid maltase leads to the accumulation of glycogen within lysosomes in various tissues, causing muscle weakness.
choiceRationales.B: Lysosomal Glucosidase is another term for acid alpha-glucosidase, and its deficiency is associated with Pompe disease, as mentioned above. Again, this primarily affects muscle cells rather than the liver.
choiceRationales.C: Muscle Phosphorylase is associated with McArdle disease, a glycogen storage disease affecting skeletal muscle. The deficiency of muscle phosphorylase leads to impaired glycogen breakdown in muscle tissue.

review.stem: A 55 year old factory worker consulted the clinic because of increasing dyspnea without cough or sputum production. He had been experiencing these for 6 months. His breath sounds were reduced in all lung fields. CXR showed dense brightly attenuated pleural mass encasing most of his left lung. Pleural biopsy specimen showed spindle and cuboidal cells invading adipose tissue. Which is the MOST likely etiologic factor in the pathogenesis of this mass?
review.explanation:
Malignant mesothelioma is a rare tumor even in individuals with a history of asbestos exposure. The tumor may appear decades after exposure, and is not related to amount or length of exposure. Bronchogenic carcinoma is more common in individuals with asbestos exposure, particularly when there is a history of smoking.
Asbestos is characterized by ferruginous bodies, yellow-brown, rod-shaped bodies with clubbed ends that stain positively with Prussian blue; these arise from iron and protein coating on fibers. Dense hyalinized fibrocalcific plaques of the parietal pleura are also present.

choiceRationales.A:
Silicosis is caused by the inhalation of silica dust. Symptoms may be absent until the disease progresses to progressive massive fibrosis. The microscopic findings typically include nodular opacities on imaging, and there may be impaired pulmonary function.
Silicosis is typified by interstitial fibrosis and causes a slight increase in the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma. However, the scenario described, with a dense pleural mass encasing the lung, is not characteristic of silicosis.
choiceRationales.B:
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP) is associated with coal dust exposure. It usually presents with nodular opacities on chest imaging, not as a dense pleural mass encasing the lung. CWP primarily affects the lung parenchyma, not the pleura.
Coal dust inhalation can lead to marked anthracosis, but without a significant risk of lung cancer.
choiceRationales.C:

Bronchogenic carcinoma is more common in individuals with asbestos exposure, particularly when there is a history of smoking.
Asbestos is characterized by ferruginous bodies, yellow-brown, rod-shaped bodies with clubbed ends that stain positively with Prussian blue; these arise from iron and protein coating on fibers. Dense hyalinized fibrocalcific plaques of the parietal pleura are also present.
choiceRationales.D:
Bird droppings are not typically associated with the development of pleural masses. Occupational exposures related to bird droppings may involve risks like fungal respiratory infections, but they are not a common cause of dense pleural masses.
Bird dust inhalation can lead to hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

She is then referred to an OBGYNE who had her fetal UTZ done at 13 weeks AOG with her uterus measuring 8x5x4 cm. She delivers her first baby full term 8 months after via spontaneous vaginal delivery. Her uterus during delivery measures 33 x 17 x 11 cm. Which cellular process contributed largely to her increase in uterine size?
review.explanation:
The adaptive growth of the uterus is a critical event that involves changes in cellular phenotypes throughout pregnancy. In early pregnancy, uterine growth is due to hyperplasia of uterine smooth muscle cells (SMCs) within the myometrium.
This study sought to test the hypothesis that the increase in myometrial growth seen during late pregnancy is due to SMC hypertrophy caused by mechanical stretch of uterine tissue by a growing fetus(es) by providing direct measurements of individual SMC size.

review.stem: A student researcher injected a chemical into his skin. Next day, he noticed an erythematous indurated area forming around the site. After two days, there was even bigger induration of about 10mm diameter. Histologically, there were many positive lymphocytes present. Which of the following reactions is MOST consistent with this appearance?
review.explanation: DTH is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction involving sensitized T cells. It typically takes 24 to 72 hours to develop after exposure to an antigen. The described scenario of erythematous induration expanding over a few days and the presence of positive lymphocytes in histology is consistent with DTH.

choiceRationales.A: The Arthus reaction is an immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. It typically occurs after the injection of an antigen into an individual who has pre-existing antibodies against that antigen. This reaction results in localized inflammation, but it is characterized by immune complex deposition and activation of complement. It doesn't usually involve lymphocytes.
choiceRationales.B: Localized anaphylaxis involves a hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE antibodies. It is characterized by the release of mast cell and basophil mediators. While it can cause localized erythema and swelling, the timeline and histological findings described are not typical for this type of reaction.
choiceRationales.C: GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells from a graft attack the host tissues. This is commonly seen after bone marrow transplantation. The described reaction doesn't match the typical presentation of GVHD, and the timeline is not consistent.
choiceRationales.D: DTH is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction involving sensitized T cells. It typically takes 24 to 72 hours to develop after exposure to an antigen. The described scenario of erythematous induration expanding over a few days and the presence of positive lymphocytes in histology is consistent with DTH.

review.stem: Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome seen upon microscopic examination of the neutrophilic nuclei in females but is absent in males. Which of the following forms of RNA plays a role in the formation of this Barr Body?
review.explanation: There are forms of noncoding RNA that play a role in gene expression. Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) segments greater than 200 nucleotides in length can bind to chromatin to restrict access of RNA polymerase to coding segments. The X chromosome transcribes XIST, a lncRNA that binds to and represses X chromosome expression. However, not all genes on the "inactive" X chromosome are switched off.

choiceRationales.A: There are forms of noncoding RNA that play a role in gene expression. Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) segments greater than 200 nucleotides in length can bind to chromatin to restrict access of RNA polymerase to coding segments. The X chromosome transcribes XIST, a lncRNA that binds to and represses X chromosome expression. However, not all genes on the "inactive" X chromosome are switched off.
choiceRationales.B: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is involved in protein synthesis. It carries the genetic information from DNA to the ribosome, where it serves as a template for protein production. Unlike lncRNA, mRNA is not directly involved in the formation of the Barr body.
choiceRationales.C: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small noncoding RNA molecules that regulate gene expression. They can bind to mRNA and inhibit its translation. However, miRNAs are not directly implicated in the formation of the Barr body.
choiceRationales.D: Transfer RNA (tRNA) is involved in protein synthesis by bringing amino acids to the ribosome based on the mRNA sequence. Similar to mRNA and miRNA, tRNA is not directly related to the formation of the Barr body.

review.stem: Why is the dysentery bloody?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disease can cause fragility of blood vessels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disease involves erosions of intestinal tissues

choices.label: C
choices.text: Organism is highly virulent and can destroy colonic mucosa

review.explanation:
Some pathogens causing dysentery, such as certain strains of Shigella, can be highly virulent and lead to significant damage to the colonic mucosa.
Shigella are resistant to gastric acid, explaining the low infective dose. Once in the intestine, organisms are taken up by M, or microfold, cells, specialized for luminal antigen sampling and presentation. The bacteria proliferate within the M cells and then escape into the lamina propria, where they are phagocytosed by and induce apoptosis of macrophages. The inflammatory response damages surface epithelium and allows Shigella within the intestinal lumen as well as those within the lamina propria to gain access to the basolateral membranes of colonic epithelial cells, across which bacteria invade the cytoplasm more efficiently than from the apical surface. All Shigella spp. carry virulence plasmids, some of which encode a type III secretion system capable of directly injecting bacterial proteins into the host cytoplasm. Shigella dysenteriae serotype 1 also release the Shiga toxin Stx, which inhibits eukaryotic protein synthesis, resulting in host cell damage and death.

choiceRationales.A: While certain diseases can affect blood vessels, dysentery, typically caused by infections, doesn't directly induce fragility of blood vessels.
choiceRationales.B: In dysentery, especially caused by invasive organisms like Shigella or Entamoeba histolytica, the infection can lead to erosions and ulcerations of the intestinal mucosa, causing bleeding. However, this statement is vague and can also apply to Entamoeba histolytica.

review.explanation: Individuals infected with V. cholerae O1 or O139 exhibit a range of clinical manifestations. Some individuals are asymptomatic or have only mild diarrhea; others present with the sudden onset of explosive and life-threatening diarrhea (cholera gravis). The stool has a characteristic appearance: a nonbilious, gray, slightly cloudy fluid with flecks of mucus, no blood, and a somewhat fishy, inoffensive odor. It has been called “rice-water” stool because of its resemblance to the water in which rice has been washed.

choiceRationales.C: Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, is associated with fever, abdominal pain, and less commonly, diarrhea. However, it doesn't typically present with the severe and profuse watery diarrhea seen in cholera.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Invades colonic mucosa and destroys it

review.explanation: Cholera is a toxin-mediated disease. The watery diarrhea characteristic of cholera is due to the action of cholera toxin, a potent protein enterotoxin elaborated by the organism in the small intestine. The toxin-coregulated pilus (TCP), so named because its synthesis is regulated in parallel with that of cholera toxin, is essential for V. cholerae to survive and multiply in (colonize) the small intestine. Cholera toxin, TCP, and several other virulence factors are coordinately regulated by ToxR. This protein modulates the expression of genes coding for virulence factors in response to environmental signals via a cascade of regulatory proteins.

choiceRationales.C: Cholera toxin, rather than a secretory peptide, is the key factor responsible for the secretory diarrhea in cholera.
choiceRationales.D: Superantigens are typically associated with immune system activation and are not the primary mechanism in cholera.

review.stem: Situation 5 - After coming from their PE class, a young high school student from a prominent family decided to end his life. He stayed overnight with the exhaust of his car aircon in full-blast and engine running in an enclosed garage. Patient is at the same time anemic and asthmatic. After 24 hours, they found him dead. After thorough investigation of the cause of death, the hospital physician concluded that the cause of death is which one of the following gases?
review.explanation: Carbon monoxide is a systemic asphyxiant that is an important cause of accidental and suicidal death. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a non-irritating, colorless, tasteless, odorless gas that is produced during any process that results in the incomplete oxidation of hydrocarbons. From the standpoint of human health, the most important environmental source of CO is the burning of carbonaceous materials, as occurs in automotive engines, furnaces, and cigarettes. In a small, closed garage, the average running car can produce sufficient CO to induce coma or death within 5 minutes, and CO concentrations can also rapidly rise to toxic levels with improper use of gasoline-powered generators (e.g., during power outages) or following mine fires.

choiceRationales.A: Nitrogen dioxide is a toxic gas, but it is not a common component of car exhaust. Exposure to high levels can cause respiratory issues, but it's not a primary component in exhaust-related suicides.
choiceRationales.B: Carbon monoxide is a systemic asphyxiant that is an important cause of accidental and suicidal death. In a small, closed garage, the average running car can produce sufficient CO to induce coma or death within 5 minutes, and CO concentrations can also rapidly rise to toxic levels with improper use of gasoline-powered generators (e.g., during power outages) or following mine fires.
choiceRationales.C: Sulfur dioxide is not a typical component of car exhaust. It is produced by burning fossil fuels containing sulfur, but it's not a primary contributor to deaths in cases like the one described.
choiceRationales.D: Argon is an inert gas and is not toxic. It is commonly used in vehicle airbags and is not produced by car engines in quantities that pose a threat to human health.

review.stem: Which one of the following reasons may not be contributory to the demise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carbon monoxide toxicity is exacerbated by exercise

choices.label: B
choices.text: He may have developed asthmatic attacks due to the fumes and exhaust of the engines

choices.label: C
choices.text: Carbon monoxide binds more to hemoglobin than oxygen leading to reduced oxygen saturation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cardiac and skeletal muscles begin to breakdown releasing creatinine kinase

review.explanation: Most probably the answer because carbon monoxide is a non-irritating, colorless, tasteless, odorless gas, which does not trigger asthma attacks. CO kills in part by inducing central nervous system (CNS) depression, which appears so insidiously that victims are often unaware of their plight.

choiceRationales.A: Exercise decreases carbon monoxide elimination half-time, although exercise and the increase in respiration would lead to increased CO exposure if CO is still present in inspired air. However, this may be unlikely because the time it takes for the garage to fill with carbon monoxide, the student has already rested from PE class, and his respiratory rate is back to normal range.
choiceRationales.B: Most probably the answer because carbon monoxide is a non-irritating, colorless, tasteless, odorless gas, which does not trigger asthma attacks. CO kills in part by inducing central nervous system (CNS) depression, which appears so insidiously that victims are often unaware of their plight.
choiceRationales.C: Hemoglobin has 200-fold greater affinity for CO than for oxygen, and the resultant carboxyhemoglobin cannot carry O2. Systemic hypoxia develops when the hemoglobin is 20% to 30% saturated with CO; unconsciousness and death are likely with 60% to 70% saturation.
choiceRationales.D: One of the complications associated with carbon monoxide toxicity is toxicity on skeletal muscle. This may cause skeletal muscle necrosis and necrotized muscles could lead to acute renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis.

review.explanation: Organophosphates are used as insecticides, medications, and nerve agents. Many "organophosphates" are potent nerve agents, functioning by inhibiting the action of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in nerve cells. They are one of the most common causes of poisoning worldwide, and are frequently intentionally used in suicides in agricultural areas. Organophosphate pesticides can be absorbed by all routes, including inhalation, ingestion, and dermal absorption. Their inhibitory effects on the acetylcholinesterase enzyme lead to a pathological excess of acetylcholine in the body.

review.explanation: Esophageal atresia is a congenital condition where the esophagus does not develop properly, resulting in a gap or discontinuity. It often presents with difficulty swallowing, excessive salivation, and vomiting.

The dorsal aortae will fuse to form the descending aorta. The proximal aorta from the aortic valve to the left carotid artery arises from the aortic sac.
choiceRationales.B: This is false. The 1st and 2nd arches largely regress by about 22 days, with the 1st aortic arch giving rise to the maxillary artery and the 2nd to the stapedial and hyoid arteries.
choiceRationales.C: This is correct. The fusion of the paired dorsal aortae contributes to the formation of the descending aorta.
choiceRationales.D:

structure in the mature circulation.

review.subject: pediatrics
review.stem: The most common major congenital heart lesion is:
review.explanation: Ventricular septal defect is one of the most common congenital heart lesions. It involves an abnormal opening in the septum (wall) between the heart's ventricles, allowing blood to flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle. VSDs vary in size and severity, and many can close on their own or require surgical intervention.

choiceRationales.A: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect characterized by four anatomical abnormalities: pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. While TOF is a significant congenital heart lesion, it is not the most common.
choiceRationales.B: Ventricular septal defect is one of the most common congenital heart lesions. It involves an abnormal opening in the septum (wall) between the heart's ventricles, allowing blood to flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle. VSDs vary in size and severity, and many can close on their own or require surgical intervention.
choiceRationales.C: Patent ductus arteriosus is a condition where the ductus arteriosus, a fetal blood vessel that connects the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta, fails to close after birth. While PDA is a common congenital heart lesion, it is not considered the most prevalent.
choiceRationales.D: Atrial septal defect is a congenital heart defect involving an abnormal opening in the septum between the heart's atria. Like VSD, ASD is a common congenital heart lesion, and the severity can vary. Some ASDs close on their own, while others may require intervention.

review.stem: Which factor establishes the diagnosis of Grave disease?
review.explanation: The presence of thyrotropin receptor-stimulating antibodies (TRSABs) is a hallmark of Graves' disease. These antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland to produce excess thyroid hormones, leading to hyperthyroidism. Testing for TRSABs, such as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs), is a crucial diagnostic marker.

choiceRationales.A: Preferential T3 elevation alone is not a specific factor for diagnosing Graves' disease. Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by hyperthyroidism, and both T3 and T4 levels are typically elevated.
choiceRationales.B: The presence of thyrotropin receptor-stimulating antibodies (TRSABs) is a hallmark of Graves' disease. These antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland to produce excess thyroid hormones, leading to hyperthyroidism. Testing for TRSABs, such as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs), is a crucial diagnostic marker.
choiceRationales.C: The presence of a goiter (enlarged thyroid gland) is a common feature of Graves' disease. The autoimmune attack on the thyroid gland, stimulated by TRSABs, leads to thyroid enlargement and increased production of thyroid hormones.
choiceRationales.D: Exophthalmos, or bulging eyes, is another characteristic feature of Graves' disease. It results from inflammation and swelling of the tissues behind the eyes, known as Graves' ophthalmopathy. While not all individuals with Graves' disease exhibit exophthalmos, its presence is a distinctive clinical sign.

review.stem: What is the MOST common bone tumor for children and adolescents beyond 10 years of age?
review.explanation: Osteosarcoma is the MOST common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents beyond 10 years of age. It typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. Osteosarcoma is characterized by the production of osteoid by malignant osteoblasts.

choiceRationales.A: The most common soft tissue sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, accounts for approximately 3.5% of childhood cancers. These tumors may occur at virtually any anatomic site but are usually found in the head and neck (25%), orbit (9%), genitourinary tract (24%), and extremities (19%); retroperitoneal and other sites account for the remainder of the primary sites. The incidence at each anatomic site is related to both patient age and tumor type.
choiceRationales.B: Osteosarcoma is the MOST common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents beyond 10 years of age. It typically arises in the metaphysis of long bones, such as the distal femur, proximal tibia, and proximal humerus. Osteosarcoma is characterized by the production of osteoid by malignant osteoblasts.
choiceRationales.C: Neuroblastoma is a malignancy that arises from neural crest cells and is more commonly found in the adrenal glands. It is not a primary bone tumor and is typically seen in early childhood.
choiceRationales.D:
Ewing sarcoma is the second most common malignant bone tumor that can affect children and adolescents. It often arises in the diaphysis of long bones, such as the femur, tibia, and humerus. Ewing sarcoma is characterized by small round cells and is the second most common primary bone tumor in this age group.
In children <10 years old, Ewing sarcoma is more common than osteosarcoma. Both tumor types are most likely to occur in the 2nd decade of life.

review.explanation: This statement is not entirely accurate. Cholera toxin primarily acts by stimulating the secretion of water and electrolytes rather than directly destroying intestinal mucosal cells.

review.explanation: The clinical diagnosis of acute bacterial sinusitis is based on history. Persistent symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection, including nasal discharge and cough, for longer than 10 days without improvement, or severe respiratory symptoms, including temperature of at least 39°C (102°F) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days, suggest a complicating acute bacterial sinusitis.

choiceRationales.B: This option is not indicative of bacterial sinusitis. Bacterial sinusitis is more likely when the nasal discharge becomes purulent, and the fever persists for an extended period.
choiceRationales.C: The clinical diagnosis of acute bacterial sinusitis is based on history. Persistent symptoms of upper respiratory tract infection, including nasal discharge and cough, for longer than 10 days without improvement, or severe respiratory symptoms, including temperature of at least 39°C (102°F) and purulent nasal discharge for 3-4 consecutive days, suggest a complicating acute bacterial sinusitis.
choiceRationales.D: This is incorrect. Symptoms such as headache, facial pain, bad breath, and pain worsening when bending forward are symptoms of both bacterial and viral sinusitis.

review.subject: pediatrics
review.stem: For uncomplicated mild to moderate bacterial sinusitis, which of the following antibiotics can be given?
review.explanation: Amoxicillin is often considered the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated bacterial sinusitis. It is a broad-spectrum penicillin derivative and is effective against many common bacterial pathogens associated with sinus infections. Amoxicillin is generally well-tolerated and has a good safety profile.

choiceRationales.A: Trimethoprim is not typically recommended as a first-line treatment for uncomplicated bacterial sinusitis. It is often used in combination with sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) and is more commonly employed for urinary tract infections and other bacterial infections. Its spectrum of activity may not cover the organisms commonly implicated in bacterial sinusitis.
choiceRationales.B: Cefixime is a third-generation cephalosporin with a broad spectrum of activity against many Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. While it can be effective against some organisms causing sinusitis, it may not be the first choice due to concerns about increasing resistance patterns and the availability of other more commonly recommended antibiotics.
choiceRationales.C: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic with a broad spectrum of activity. It is effective against many respiratory pathogens, including some commonly implicated in sinusitis. However, its use is sometimes limited due to increasing antibiotic resistance and the potential for side effects. It may be considered in cases of penicillin allergy.
choiceRationales.D: Amoxicillin is often considered the first-line antibiotic for uncomplicated bacterial sinusitis. It is a broad-spectrum penicillin derivative and is effective against many common bacterial pathogens associated with sinus infections. Amoxicillin is generally well-tolerated and has a good safety profile.

review.stem: Which characteristics distinguish this bacteria from the rest of other bacteria?
review.explanation: Vibrio cholera is oxidase positive. This means that the bacterium produces the enzyme oxidase, which can be detected using an oxidase test. The oxidase test is commonly used to differentiate between bacterial genera, and a positive result indicates the presence of certain respiratory enzymes. Among the notable bacteria that cause diarrhea, Vibrio is the only oxidase positive bacteria.

choiceRationales.A: Vibrio cholera is motile. It possesses a single, polar flagellum that enables it to move actively in aqueous environments. Motility is a characteristic feature of Vibrio species, allowing them to navigate in aquatic environments, which is relevant to their transmission. However, Motility alone does not distinguish Vibrio from other bacteria.
choiceRationales.B: Vibrio cholera is oxidase positive. This means that the bacterium produces the enzyme oxidase, which can be detected using an oxidase test. The oxidase test is commonly used to differentiate between bacterial genera, and a positive result indicates the presence of certain respiratory enzymes. Among the notable bacteria that cause diarrhea, Vibrio is the only oxidase positive bacteria.
choiceRationales.C: Vibrio cholera is a Gram-negative bacterium. The Gram-negative classification is based on the structure of the bacterial cell wall. In the case of Vibrio cholera, its cell wall structure includes an outer membrane, which is a characteristic feature of Gram-negative bacteria. However, Gram staining alone does not distinguish Vibrio from other bacteria.
choiceRationales.D: Vibrio cholera is not a lactose fermenter. Unlike some Enterobacteriaceae, such as Escherichia coli, which ferment lactose, Vibrio cholera does not possess the necessary enzymes to utilize lactose.

review.stem: What is TRUE regarding medications of dysmenorrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medication is needed before the first day of menses

review.explanation: Treatment for primary dysmenorrhea is aimed at decreasing levels of prostaglandins, preferably before they are produced. Thus, the mainstay treatment is with prostaglandin synthetase inhibition by either nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, hormonal contraception, or a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist beginning at, or preferably the day prior to, menstruation. The high doses of around the clock treatment are rarely needed for more than the first 2 days.

choiceRationales.A: Treatment for primary dysmenorrhea is aimed at decreasing levels of prostaglandins, preferably before they are produced. Thus, the mainstay treatment is with prostaglandin synthetase inhibition by either nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, hormonal contraception, or a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist beginning at, or preferably the day prior to, menstruation. The high doses of around the clock treatment are rarely needed for more than the first 2 days.
choiceRationales.B: While the initiation of medication before the first day of menses is often recommended, the duration of medication use, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or other treatments, varies based on individual response and the severity of symptoms. For some individuals, taking medication until the last day of menstruation may be necessary to ensure sustained relief from pain and discomfort.
choiceRationales.C: In general, medication use beyond the last day of menstruation is not a routine practice for primary dysmenorrhea. However, individual cases may vary, and if symptoms persist or recur beyond the menstrual period, further evaluation may be necessary. The goal is to tailor the duration of medication to the specific needs of the patient.
choiceRationales.D: This is generally false. Medications are usually started prior to the first day of menses and are needed up to 2 days of menses.

review.stem: Situation 13 – A 3 years old boy was admitted to the Pediatric Emergency room for abdominal enlargement. Physical examination also revealed facial and bipedal edema. Immediately a urinalysis was ordered revealing proteinuria of 3+ and microscopic hematuria. What is NOT indicated in the triad of clinical findings for Nephrotic Syndrome?
review.explanation: Hypertension is not typically a part of the classic presentation of nephrotic syndrome. However, it's essential to monitor blood pressure regularly in pediatric patients with nephrotic syndrome as secondary hypertension can occur, possibly due to renal parenchymal disease or the use of corticosteroids.

choiceRationales.A: Nephrotic syndrome is associated with dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated levels of cholesterol and triglycerides. This occurs as a result of altered lipid metabolism in the liver, influenced by the urinary loss of proteins, particularly albumin.
choiceRationales.B: A hallmark of nephrotic syndrome is a reduction in serum albumin levels. The loss of albumin through the urine, often accompanied by other proteins, contributes to a decrease in the oncotic pressure within the vascular system, leading to the development of edema.

review.stem: Juan has been diagnosed with rheumatic heart disease. ECG of Juan revealed atrial fibrillation. The consultant started Juan on Digoxin. Select the rationale for such medication.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase conductivity of the AV node

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

review.explanation: This is correct. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside that primarily acts by inhibiting the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, which is responsible for maintaining the balance of sodium and potassium ions in cardiac myocytes. By inhibiting this pump, Digoxin increases intracellular sodium levels, leading to a subsequent increase in intracellular calcium concentration. The elevated calcium levels enhance cardiac contractility (positive inotropic effect) and also contribute to increased vagal tone, leading to a negative chronotropic effect (slowing of the heart rate). Digoxin's effects on contractility and heart rate are particularly beneficial in conditions like heart failure and atrial fibrillation.

By doing so, Digoxin helps to control the heart rate in conditions like atrial fibrillation, where there is uncoordinated atrial activity. Slowing the AV node conduction can improve ventricular filling and cardiac output.
choiceRationales.B: Digoxin affects the SA node and automaticity of the heart by decreasing the firing rate of the SA node, lowering the overall heartrate.
choiceRationales.C: Digoxin does not directly increase the excitability of the atria and ventricles. Its effects are more focused on the AV node and the contractility of the myocardium.

review.subject: pharmacology
review.stem: Which of the following is an effect notable with the use of general anesthesia?
review.explanation:
Halothane, enflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane all depress normal cardiac contractility (halothane and enflurane more so than isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane). As a result, all volatile agents tend to decrease mean arterial pressure in direct proportion to their alveolar concentration. With halothane and enflurane, the reduced arterial pressure is caused primarily by myocardial depression (reduced cardiac output) and there is little change in systemic vascular resistance. In contrast, isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane produce greater vasodilation with minimal effect on cardiac output. These differences may have important implications for patients with heart failure. Because isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane better preserve cardiac output as well as reduce preload (ventricular filling) and afterload (systemic vascular resistance), these agents may be better choices for patients with impaired myocardial function.
Nitrous oxide also depresses myocardial function in a concentration-dependent manner. This depression may be significantly offset by a concomitant activation of the sympathetic nervous system resulting in preservation of cardiac output. Therefore, administration of nitrous oxide in combination with the more potent volatile anesthetics can minimize circulatory depressant effects by both anesthetic-sparing and sympathetic-activating actions.

choiceRationales.B: This is generally incorrect. General anesthesia typically involves CNS depression rather than excitation. Anesthetics act on the central nervous system to induce a state of unconsciousness and reduced sensory perception.
choiceRationales.C: This is generally incorrect. General anesthesia tends to decrease renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate. Anesthesia-induced changes in hemodynamics can impact renal function.

With halothane and enflurane, the reduced arterial pressure is caused primarily by myocardial depression (reduced cardiac output) and there is little change in systemic vascular resistance. In contrast, isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane produce greater vasodilation with minimal effect on cardiac output. These differences may have important implications for patients with heart failure. Because isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane better preserve cardiac output as well as reduce preload (ventricular filling) and afterload (systemic vascular resistance), these agents may be better choices for patients with impaired myocardial function.
Nitrous oxide also depresses myocardial function in a concentration-dependent manner. This depression may be significantly offset by a concomitant activation of the sympathetic nervous system resulting in preservation of cardiac output. Therefore, administration of nitrous oxide in combination with the more potent volatile anesthetics can minimize circulatory depressant effects by both anesthetic-sparing and sympathetic-activating actions.

review.stem: Identify the drug that inhibits the conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain thereby decreasing the side effect and increasing the available levodopa for transport inside the brain:
review.explanation: Carbidopa is a peripheral inhibitor of dopa decarboxylase, an enzyme that converts levodopa to dopamine in peripheral tissues outside the brain. While it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, it plays a crucial role in the treatment of Parkinson's disease when administered in combination with levodopa. By inhibiting the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, more levodopa reaches the brain, where it can be converted to dopamine and alleviate the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

choiceRationales.A: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist and does not inhibit the conversion of levodopa to dopamine. It works by directly stimulating dopamine receptors.
choiceRationales.B: Tolcapone is a catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor. It inhibits the enzyme COMT, which is responsible for the breakdown of levodopa. By inhibiting COMT, tolcapone increases the bioavailability of levodopa and its duration of action.
choiceRationales.C: Carbidopa is a peripheral inhibitor of dopa decarboxylase, an enzyme that converts levodopa to dopamine in peripheral tissues outside the brain. While it does not cross the blood-brain barrier, it plays a crucial role in the treatment of Parkinson's disease when administered in combination with levodopa. By inhibiting the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, more levodopa reaches the brain, where it can be converted to dopamine and alleviate the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
choiceRationales.D: Selegiline is a monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B) inhibitor. It reduces the breakdown of dopamine in the brain but does not directly affect the peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine.

Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with activity against a broad spectrum of bacteria, including Leptospira. However, it is not a recommended first-line treatment for leptospirosis.
At first glance, the fluoroquinolones seem like ideal therapy for leptospirosis. They are active against numerous Leptospira serovars in vitro, and their broad spectrum of activity allows coverage of other diseases that may be considered in differential diagnosis. To our knowledge, only two prior investigations have examined their use in animal models, and these gave conflicting results, likely because of methodological differences.

review.subject: physiology
review.stem: The retinal area that does not respond to light is:
review.explanation:
This is the correct anatomical answer. The optic disc is the precise location on the retina where the blind spot is located. It lacks photoreceptor cells and is therefore insensitive to light. As a result, this area of the visual field is not perceived by the individual.
The blind spot in humans is located about 12–15° temporally and 1.5° below the horizontal and is roughly 7.5° high and 5.5° wide.

choiceRationales.A: A blind spot, scotoma, is an obscuration of the visual field. A particular blind spot known as the physiological blind spot, "blind point", or punctum caecum in medical literature, is the place in the visual field that corresponds to the lack of light-detecting photoreceptor cells on the optic disc of the retina where the optic nerve passes through the optic disc. Because there are no cells to detect light on the optic disc, the corresponding part of the field of vision is invisible. Via processes in the brain, the blind spot is interpolated based on surrounding detail and information from the other eye, so it is not normally perceived.
choiceRationales.B: The macula is a small, specialized area in the retina responsible for central and high-acuity vision. It contains a high density of cone cells, which are photoreceptors sensitive to bright light and responsible for color vision. Unlike the blind spot, the macula is a region of the retina that actively responds to light and is crucial for detailed vision.
choiceRationales.C:
This is the correct anatomical answer. The optic disc is the precise location on the retina where the blind spot is located. It lacks photoreceptor cells and is therefore insensitive to light. As a result, this area of the visual field is not perceived by the individual.
The blind spot in humans is located about 12–15° temporally and 1.5° below the horizontal and is roughly 7.5° high and 5.5° wide.
choiceRationales.D: The fovea is a small, central pit within the macula that contains a high concentration of cone cells. It is the area of the retina responsible for the sharpest vision and is essential for tasks requiring visual detail. Unlike the blind spot, the fovea actively responds to light and is a critical region for visual acuity.

review.subject: physiology
review.stem: K+ secretion by the renal distal tubule will be decreased by:
review.explanation: Spironolactone acts by antagonizing the response of the distal tubule to aldosterone. This decreases the ability of aldosterone to stimulate distal potassium secretion.

choiceRationales.A: Spironolactone acts by antagonizing the response of the distal tubule to aldosterone. This decreases the ability of aldosterone to stimulate distal potassium secretion.
choiceRationales.B: Metabolic alkalosis tends to decrease potassium secretion in the renal tubules. In alkalosis, there is an increased uptake of hydrogen ions (H+) by cells in exchange for potassium ions (K+). This shift of potassium into cells reduces the concentration of potassium in the tubular fluid, leading to decreased potassium secretion.
choiceRationales.C: Increased dietary potassium intake stimulates potassium secretion by several mechanisms. It enhances the activity of the Na-K-ATPase pump, increasing potassium uptake across the basolateral membrane. Additionally, higher extracellular fluid (ECF) potassium concentrations stimulate potassium secretion. The increased gradient from renal interstitial fluid to the interior of epithelial cells reduces backleakage of potassium from inside the cells, contributing to increased potassium secretion.
choiceRationales.D: Hyperaldosteronism, an excessive secretion of aldosterone, enhances potassium secretion in the distal tubule. Aldosterone increases the number of potassium channels in the luminal membrane, promoting potassium secretion. This leads to an increased excretion of potassium in the urine.

review.subject: physiology
review.stem: Anemia in CKD-in-uremia is due to:
review.explanation: Folate deficiency has been implicated as a contributory factor in renal anemia and hyporesponsiveness to rHuEPO treatment. A normocytic, normochromic anemia is observed as early as stage 3 CKD and is almost universal by stage 4. The primary cause in patients with CKD is insufficient production of erythropoietin (EPO) by the diseased kidneys. Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) is a less recognized, but potentially significant cause of renal anemia in CKD patients. Several changes that occur in bone and mineral metabolism result in overproduction of PTH. Patients with SHPT, usually associated with osteitis fibrosa on bone histology, show considerable resistance to EPO, which is partly because of replacement of the bone marrow by fibrous tissue.

choiceRationales.A: Folic acid deficiency can contribute to anemia, but in the context of chronic kidney disease (CKD), the primary cause of anemia is not folic acid deficiency. The anemia seen in CKD is primarily attributed to insufficient production of erythropoietin (EPO) by the diseased kidneys.
choiceRationales.B: Blood loss is not a typical cause of anemia in chronic kidney disease. In CKD, the anemia is primarily related to impaired erythropoietin production and other factors associated with kidney dysfunction.
choiceRationales.C: Folate deficiency has been implicated as a contributory factor in renal anemia and hyporesponsiveness to rHuEPO treatment. Patients with SHPT, usually associated with osteitis fibrosa on bone histology, show considerable resistance to EPO, which is partly because of replacement of the bone marrow by fibrous tissue.
choiceRationales.D: Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT) is mentioned as a potentially significant cause of renal anemia in CKD patients. Changes in bone and mineral metabolism in SHPT can result in the overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Patients with SHPT may show resistance to EPO, partly due to the replacement of bone marrow by fibrous tissue.

review.subject: physiology
review.stem: Which substance has the highest renal clearance?
review.explanation: The significance of the clearance depends on the substance used. The clearance of inulin, which is entirely filtered, defines the GFR; and the clearance of para-aminohippurate (PAH), which is both filtered (~90%) and secreted by the tubules, defines renal plasma flow.

choiceRationales.A: Sodium is primarily reabsorbed in the renal tubules, and only a small fraction is excreted. The renal clearance of sodium is lower compared to substances that are filtered more freely and excreted more extensively.
choiceRationales.B: The significance of the clearance depends on the substance used. The clearance of inulin, which is entirely filtered, defines the GFR; and the clearance of para-aminohippurate (PAH), which is both filtered (~90%) and secreted by the tubules, defines renal plasma flow.
choiceRationales.C: Inulin is a substance that is entirely filtered by the glomerulus and is not reabsorbed or secreted by the tubules. The clearance of inulin is used to define the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), making it a valuable marker for assessing kidney function.
choiceRationales.D: Glucose is typically completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubules under normal physiological conditions. In healthy individuals, there should be no significant glucose excretion in the urine. If glucose is present in the urine, it may indicate a malfunction in glucose reabsorption mechanisms.

review.explanation:
There are four reservoirs of oxygen in the body which one can potentially access as a source of metabolic fuel. These are:
Dissolved oxygen as molecules of O2 in blood and generally in body water
Bound gas, complexed with other molecules:
Bound to haemoglobin
Bound to myoglobin
Bound to other molecules
Gas in cavities, particularly in the lungs:
FRC is the most clinically important of these reservoirs

review.subject: physiology
review.stem: Which of the following causes of hypoxemia is characterized by a decreased arterial PO2 and in increased A-a gradient?
review.explanation: A right-to-left cardiac shunt is associated with an increased A-a gradient, reflecting a lack of O2 equilibration between alveolar gas and systemic arterial blood. In a right-to-left shunt, a portion of the right heart output or pulmonary blood flow is not oxygenated in the lungs, which "dilutes" the PO2 of the normally oxygenated blood. With hypoventilation and ascent to high altitude, both alveolar and arterial PO2 are decreased, but the A-a gradient is normal.

choiceRationales.A: Anemia is a cause of decreased O2 content in the blood due to a decreased hemoglobin concentration. However, anemia is not typically associated with an increased alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient. The A-a gradient is a measure of the difference in oxygen partial pressure between the alveoli (in the lungs) and the arterial blood.
choiceRationales.B: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning decreases the oxygen-binding capacity of hemoglobin by forming carboxyhemoglobin. While it results in decreased arterial PO2, it is not associated with an increased A-a gradient. Carbon monoxide poisoning can cause a leftward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve, impairing oxygen release to tissues.
choiceRationales.C: A right-to-left cardiac shunt is associated with an increased A-a gradient, reflecting a lack of O2 equilibration between alveolar gas and systemic arterial blood. In a right-to-left shunt, a portion of the right heart output or pulmonary blood flow is not oxygenated in the lungs, which "dilutes" the PO2 of the normally oxygenated blood. With hypoventilation and ascent to high altitude, both alveolar and arterial PO2 are decreased, but the A-a gradient is normal.
choiceRationales.D: Ascent to high altitude is a cause of decreased alveolar and arterial PO2. However, it is not typically associated with an increased A-a gradient. In high-altitude conditions, both alveolar and arterial PO2 decrease, but the A-a gradient remains normal.

D. Ascent to high place

review.explanation: This statement is correct. Spinal shock is typically a transient phenomenon that occurs immediately following spinal cord injury or resection. choiceRationales.A: This is a potential outcome following spinal cord resection. choiceRationales.B: This is a characteristic feature of spinal shock, which may occur following spinal cord resection. Spinal shock is a temporary physiological state characterized by a loss of reflexes, flaccid paralysis, and sensory loss below the level of the injury. During spinal shock, reflexes such as the bulbocavernosus reflex may be absent.
choiceRationales.C: This is another possible consequence of spinal cord resection. Damage to the spinal cord can disrupt the normal functioning of the nerves that control bladder function, leading to urinary retention. Patients may experience difficulty urinating or incomplete bladder emptying due to loss of muscle tone in the bladder and impaired coordination of bladder contraction and relaxation.

review.stem: With carbon dioxide diffusion from tissues to the plasma then to blood cell, hemoglobin-CO2 facilitates oxygen offloading and this process is known as .
review.explanation: As the blood passes through the tissues, CO2 diffuses from the tissue cells into the blood. This diffusion increases the blood PCO2, which in turn raises the blood H2CO3 (carbonic acid) and the hydrogen ion concentration. These effects shift the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right and downward, forcing O2 away from the hemoglobin (oxygen offloading) and therefore delivering increased amounts of O2 to the tissues.

choiceRationales.A: The Michaelis-Menten theory is related to enzyme kinetics. It describes the relationship between the rate of a reaction and the concentration of a substrate, typically in the context of enzyme-catalyzed reactions. This theory is not directly relevant to the process of oxygen offloading facilitated by hemoglobin and carbon dioxide.
choiceRationales.B: The Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium relates to the distribution of ions across a semipermeable membrane, especially in the context of cells and plasma. It is not specifically associated with the process of oxygen offloading facilitated by hemoglobin and carbon dioxide.
choiceRationales.C: The Haldane effect refers to the phenomenon where the oxygenation of hemoglobin decreases its affinity for carbon dioxide. In other words, when hemoglobin binds with oxygen, it releases its hold on carbon dioxide, facilitating the unloading of CO2 from the blood. This effect is particularly relevant in the tissues where oxygen is needed, and CO2 produced in metabolism needs to be transported back to the lungs.
choiceRationales.D: As the blood passes through the tissues, CO2 diffuses from the tissue cells into the blood. This diffusion increases the blood PCO2, which in turn raises the blood H2CO3 (carbonic acid) and the hydrogen ion concentration. These effects shift the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right and downward, forcing O2 away from the hemoglobin (oxygen offloading) and therefore delivering increased amounts of O2 to the tissues.

review.stem: Hyperventilating at an altitude will bring:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kidney to produce angiotensin to keep the patient’s BP to normal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Respiratory quotient will be driven below one

choices.label: C
choices.text: Faster fall in the carbonic acid levels than that of the CO2

review.explanation: This statement is correct. Hyperventilation at altitude leads to respiratory alkalosis, characterized by an increase in blood pH. The elimination of CO2 through hyperventilation reduces the concentration of carbonic acid in the blood, shifting the bicarbonate buffer system towards alkalinity and resulting in an increase in blood pH.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is not accurate in the context of hyperventilating at altitude. Angiotensin is primarily involved in regulating blood pressure by vasoconstriction and aldosterone release. However, hyperventilation at altitude primarily affects respiratory and acid-base balance, rather than directly influencing the kidney's production of angiotensin.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is incorrect. The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed during metabolism. Hyperventilation leads to a decrease in CO2 levels, which may lower the RQ, but it typically does not drive it below one. A value below one would suggest a predominance of fat metabolism, which is not typically observed during hyperventilation.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is incorrect. Carbonic acid (H2CO3) is formed from the hydration of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the blood. Hyperventilation causes a decrease in CO2 levels, leading to a decrease in carbonic acid levels. However, the rate of decrease in carbonic acid levels is proportional to the rate of decrease in CO2 levels, so there is no disparity between the two.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is correct. Hyperventilation at altitude leads to respiratory alkalosis, characterized by an increase in blood pH. The elimination of CO2 through hyperventilation reduces the concentration of carbonic acid in the blood, shifting the bicarbonate buffer system towards alkalinity and resulting in an increase in blood pH.
