review.stem: Surgical management of the wound is also a critical determinant of the propensity to develop a surgical infection. Closure of an appendectomy wound in a patient with perforated appendicitis who is receiving appropriate antibiotics will result in a wound infection in what percentage of patients?
review.explanation: Surgical management of the wound is also a critical determinant of the propensity to develop a surgical site infection (SSI). In healthy individuals, class I and II wounds may be closed primarily, while skin closure of class III and IV wounds is associated with high rates of incisional SSIs (~25% to 50%). The superficial aspects of these latter types of wounds should be packed open and allowed to heal by secondary intention, although selective use of delayed primary closure has been associated with a reduction in incisional SSI rates. It remains to be determined whether National Nosocomial Infections Surveillance System (NNIS)-type stratification schemes can be employed prospectively in order to target specific subgroups of patients who will benefit from the use of prophylactic antibiotic and/or specific wound management techniques. One clear example based on cogent data from clinical trials is that class III wounds in healthy patients undergoing appendectomy for perforated or gangrenous appendicitis can be primarily closed as long as antibiotic therapy directed against aerobes and anaerobes is administered. This practice leads to SSI rates of approximately 3% to 4%.

choiceRationales.A: This range is not typically associated with wound infection rates in the context of appropriate surgical management and antibiotic therapy. Surgical site infection rates can be influenced by various factors, including the type of surgery, patient characteristics, and the presence of comorbidities.
choiceRationales.B: This range is higher than the typical rates associated with appropriate wound management and antibiotic therapy. In the context of perforated appendicitis, the goal is to minimize the risk of surgical site infection through a combination of appropriate surgical technique, antibiotic administration, and wound care.
choiceRationales.C: Surgical management of the wound is also a critical determinant of the propensity to develop a surgical site infection (SSI). review.stem: The avoidance of prolonged orotracheal and nasotracheal intubation decreases the risk of laryngeal and subglottic injury and potential stenosis. Which of the following is NOT true about tracheostomy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improves patient discomfort as compared to long term oropharyngeal intubation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Should be performed in patients anticipated to be intubated more than 2 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Does not obligate patient to loss of speech

choices.label: D
choices.text: Usually spontaneously closes within 2 months of removal

review.explanation: The avoidance of prolonged orotracheal intubation decreases the risk of laryngeal and subglottic injury and potential stenosis, facilitates oral and pulmonary suctioning, and decreases patient discomfort. When the tracheostomy is no longer needed, the tube is removed and closure of the opening usually occurs spontaneously over a 2-week period. Placement of a tracheostomy does not obligate a patient to loss of speech. When a large-cuffed tracheostomy tube is in place, expecting a patient to be capable of normal speech is impractical. However, after a patient is downsized to an uncuffed tracheostomy tube, intermittent finger occlusion or Pass-Muir valve placement will allow a patient to communicate while using the tracheostomy to bypass the upper airway.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is true. Tracheostomy can improve patient comfort compared to prolonged orotracheal intubation. Tracheostomy allows for better oral care, reduces the risk of laryngeal and subglottic injury, and facilitates suctioning, contributing to improved patient comfort.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is generally true. Tracheostomy is often considered in patients who are anticipated to require prolonged mechanical ventilation, typically beyond 2 weeks. It offers advantages in terms of airway management, patient comfort, and decreased risk of complications associated with prolonged endotracheal intubation.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is true. While speech may be temporarily affected, especially with larger-cuffed tracheostomy tubes, downsizing to an uncuffed tube or using techniques like finger occlusion or Pass-Muir valve placement allows patients to communicate effectively while using the tracheostomy.
choiceRationales.D: The avoidance of prolonged orotracheal intubation decreases the risk of laryngeal and subglottic injury and potential stenosis, facilitates oral and pulmonary suctioning, and decreases patient discomfort. review.stem: You were assigned to monitor post-operative patients on catheter. Which of the following is NOT TRUE regarding intravascular catheter infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacteria with gram negative bacteria or fungi should prompt catheter removal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many patients with intravascular catheter infections are asymptomatic

choices.label: C
choices.text: In high-risk patients, prophylactic antibiotics infused through the catheter can reduce rate of catheter infections

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selected low-virulence infections can be treated with a prolonged course of antibiotics.

review.explanation:
This is NOT TRUE.
Many patients who develop intravascular catheter infections are asymptomatic, often exhibiting solely an elevation in the blood white blood cell (WBC) count. Blood cultures obtained from a peripheral site and drawn through the catheter that reveal the presence of the same organism increase the index of suspicion for the presence of a catheter infection. Obvious purulence at the exit site of the skin tunnel, severe sepsis syndrome due to any type of organism when other potential causes have been excluded, or bacteremia due to gram-negative aerobes or fungi should lead to catheter removal. Selected catheter infections due to low-virulence microbes such as Staphylococcus epidermidis can be effectively treated in approximately 50% to 60% of patients with a 14- to 21-day course of an antibiotic, which should be considered when no other vascular access site exists. Use of systemic antibacterial or antifungal agents to prevent catheter infection is of no utility and is contraindicated.

choiceRationales.A: This is TRUE. Obvious purulence at the exit site of the skin tunnel, severe sepsis syndrome due to any type of organism when other potential causes have been excluded, or bacteremia due to gram-negative aerobes or fungi should prompt catheter removal. This is crucial to prevent the spread of infection and further complications.
choiceRationales.B: This is TRUE. Many patients who develop intravascular catheter infections are asymptomatic. In some cases, the only indicator may be an elevation in the blood white blood cell (WBC) count. This highlights the importance of vigilant monitoring and considering diagnostic tests, even in the absence of obvious clinical symptoms.

choiceRationales.D:
This is TRUE.
Selected catheter infections due to low-virulence microbes, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, can be effectively treated in approximately 50% to 60% of patients with a 14- to 21-day course of an appropriate antibiotic. This is a valid approach, especially when no other vascular access site exists, and it aligns with the principles of tailored antibiotic therapy based on the specific characteristics of the infection.

review.stem: Which of the body is NOT likely to contain resident microorganisms?
review.explanation: The urogenital, biliary, pancreatic ductal, and distal respiratory tracts do not possess resident microflora in healthy individuals, although microbes may be present if these barriers are affected by disease (eg, malignancy, inflammation, calculi, or foreign body), or if microorganisms are introduced from an external source (eg, urinary catheter or pulmonary aspiration). In contrast, a significant number of microbes are encountered in many portions of the gastrointestinal tract, with vast numbers being found within the oropharynx and distal colorectum, although the specific organisms differ.

choiceRationales.A: The nares (nostrils) are a common site for the colonization of microorganisms, including various bacteria. Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), is one of the bacteria commonly found in the nares.
choiceRationales.B: The terminal ileum, which is part of the small intestine, is populated by a variety of microorganisms, particularly in the lower gastrointestinal tract. The gut microbiota, including various bacteria, plays a crucial role in digestion and maintaining gut health.
choiceRationales.C: The oropharynx, located at the back of the throat, is a site rich in resident microorganisms, including bacteria. Common bacteria found in the oropharynx include Streptococcus species.
choiceRationales.D: The urogenital, biliary, pancreatic ductal, and distal respiratory tracts do not possess resident microflora in healthy individuals, although microbes may be present if these barriers are affected by disease (eg, malignancy, inflammation, calculi, or foreign body), or if microorganisms are introduced from an external source (eg, urinary catheter or pulmonary aspiration). review.stem: Which of the following is the MOST effective post-exposure prophylaxis for a surgeon stuck with a needle while operating on an HIV-positive patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There is no effective treatment known

choices.label: B
choices.text: Single drug therapy started within 24 hours of exposure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two- or three- drug therapy started within hours of exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triple drug therapy started within 24 hours of exposure

review.explanation:
Most occupationally acquired HIV infection has been documented in nurses or laboratory technicians. Postexposure drug prophylaxis should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within 2 h. In cases where the status of the source is unknown, standard serologic testing (enzyme immunoassay and Western blot) is indicated, but the results may take several days. A rapid HIV test can now give results within 1 h. However, serologic test results may be negative in infected individuals for 3 to 12 weeks following the acquisition of the virus. The decision to start postexposure drug prophylaxis must therefore consider any known risk factors that the source may have, regardless of the serologic results.
Postexposure prophylaxis consists of multidrug therapy with a combination of nucleoside and protease inhibitors. Adverse side effects are frequent and sometimes severe. Recommendations for postexposure prophylaxis continue to evolve.
The most effective method of reducing the risk for transmission of HIV to a person stuck with a needle from a known HIV-positive patient is to begin combined triple antiretroviral therapy. The first dose should be given after exposure as soon as possible. Besides a baseline HIV test, this person should undergo an additional follow-up testing at both 3 and 6 months.

choiceRationales.A: There is post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) available for individuals who have been exposed to HIV. PEP involves the use of antiretroviral medications to reduce the risk of HIV transmission after a potential exposure.
choiceRationales.B: While early initiation of PEP is crucial, the most effective approach involves the use of combination therapy (multiple drugs) rather than a single drug. This is because HIV can quickly develop resistance to a single drug, and combination therapy helps prevent this.
choiceRationales.C: This is a more effective option. PEP typically involves the use of two or three antiretroviral drugs started as soon as possible after exposure. The combination helps target different stages of the HIV life cycle and reduces the risk of transmission.

review.stem: What is the etiology associated with a holosystolic murmur that is accompanied by ventricular septal defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crescendo-decrescendo, occurs as blood is ejected into left and right ventricular outflow tracts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flow between chambers that have widely different pressures throughout systole

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ventricular filling that follows atrial contraction

choices.label: D
choices.text: A relative disproportion between valve orifice size and diastolic-blood flow volume

review.explanation:
This is correct.
A holosystolic murmur with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) is typically caused by flow between chambers with widely different pressures throughout systole. The VSD allows blood to flow from the higher-pressure left ventricle to the lower-pressure right ventricle during systole, leading to a continuous murmur throughout the entire systolic phase.

choiceRationales.A: This description is characteristic of an ejection systolic murmur, often associated with Mitral stenosis, Mitral Regurgitation, Tricuspid Stenosis or Tricuspid insufficiency, not a holosystolic murmur.
choiceRationales.B:
This is correct.
A holosystolic murmur with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) is typically caused by flow between chambers with widely different pressures throughout systole. review.stem: The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency. Which bypass conduit has the highest patency rate?
review.explanation: Bypass Conduit Selection. The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency. The conduit with the highest patency rate (98% at 5 years and 85%–90% at 10 years) is the internal thoracic artery which is most commonly left attached proximally to the subclavian artery (although occasionally used as a free graft) and anastomosed distally to the target coronary artery. The use of both internal thoracic arteries has been shown to increase event-free survival in a number of studies.

choiceRationales.A: Bypass Conduit Selection. The most important criterion in conduit selection is graft patency. The conduit with the highest patency rate (98% at 5 years and 85%–90% at 10 years) is the internal thoracic artery which is most commonly left attached proximally to the subclavian artery (although occasionally used as a free graft) and anastomosed distally to the target coronary artery. The use of both internal thoracic arteries has been shown to increase event-free survival in a number of studies.
choiceRationales.B:
The patency of the greater saphenous vein is generally lower compared to the internal thoracic artery.
The greater saphenous vein is a commonly used conduit in coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) procedures. While it is widely used, its patency rates may not match those of the internal thoracic artery.
choiceRationales.C:
The radial artery also offers good patency rates.
The radial artery is another arterial conduit option for CABG. It has been used as a graft with favorable outcomes, although its patency rates may vary.
choiceRationales.D:
The patency rate of the gastroepiploic artery is generally good.
The gastroepiploic artery is an alternative arterial conduit, often used when other conduits are not suitable. It can be attached to the right coronary artery or other vessels.

review.stem: Ischemic strokes are due to hypoperfusion from arterial occlusion or to decreased flow resulting from proximal arterial stenosis and poor collateral network. Which of the following is the most common cause of ischemic stroke?
review.explanation: Approximately 700,000 Americans suffer an annual or recurrent stroke each year. Eighty-five percent of all strokes are ischemic and 15% are hemorrhagic. Common causes of ischemic stroke are cardiogenic emboli in 35%, carotid artery stenosis in 30%, lacunar in 10%, miscellaneous in 10%, and idiopathic in 15%. The term "cerebrovascular accident" is often used interchangeably to refer to an ischemic stroke. The severity of carotid artery stenosis is a strong predictor for stroke, with more severe occlusive disease associated with a higher incidence of stroke. A prior history of neurologic symptoms such as TIA or stroke is an important determinant for recurrent ipsilateral stroke.

review.stem: Angina pectoris is the pain or discomfort caused by myocardial ischemia. Which of the following BEST describes angina pectoris?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Typical" angina occurs in approximately 50% of patients with coronary disease.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Angina is typically substernal and may radiate to the left upper extremity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Atypical" angina occurs more commonly in men.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Angina is a typical symptom for mitral stenosis.

review.explanation:
Angina pectoris, the most common clinical manifestation of coronary artery disease (CAD), results from an imbalance between myocardial O2 supply and demand, most often due to atherosclerotic coronary artery obstruction.
Angina is usually characterized more as a discomfort rather than pain. Terms frequently used by patients include squeezing, tightness, pressure, constriction, strangling, burning, heartburn, fullness in the chest, band-like sensation, knot in the center of the chest, lump in throat, ache, heavy weight on chest (elephant sitting on chest), like a bra too tight, and toothache (when there is radiation to the lower jaw.
Angina is referred to the corresponding dermatomes (C5-6 and T1-T6) that supply afferent nerves to the same segments of the spinal cord as the heart. Thus, angina often radiates to other parts of the body, including the upper abdomen (epigastric), shoulders, arms (upper and forearm), wrist, fingers, neck and throat, lower jaw and teeth (but not upper jaw), and rarely to the back (specifically the interscapular region).
Atypical angina is more common in women than in men.

choiceRationales.A:
Coronary heart disease impacts over 17 million adults in the United States. Of the 17 million Americans affected, 55% of those are male. It contributes to over 500,000 deaths each year in the U.S. At age 40 years, the lifetime risk of developing coronary disease is estimated at 49% for men and 32% for women.
Angina therefore afflicts 58% of patients with CAD. Approximately 500,000 new cases are reported yearly, and prevalence rises rapidly with increasing age. While anginal attacks are considered reversible short term, they are by no means benign, with significant morbidity and mortality.

review.stem: Which is the MOST accurate diagnostic test for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)?
review.explanation: All patients with gastrinoma have an elevated gastrin level, and hypergastrinemia in the presence of elevated basal acid output (BAO) strongly suggests gastrinoma. Patients with gastrinoma usually have a BAO > 15 mEq/h or >5 mEq/h if they have had a previous procedure for peptic ulcer. Acid secretory medications should be held for several days before gastrin measurement, because acid suppression may falsely elevate gastrin levels. Causes of hypergastrinemia can be divided into those associated with hyperacidity and those associated with hypoacidity (see Fig. 26-1). The diagnosis of ZES is confirmed by the secretin stimulation test. An intravenous (IV) bolus of secretin (2 U/kg) is given, and gastrin levels are checked before and after injection. An increase in serum gastrin of 200 pg/mL or greater suggests the presence of gastrinoma.

CT scans are valuable for imaging structures in the abdomen but are not the primary diagnostic test for ZES.

choiceRationales.C:
Fasting serum gastrin is a key diagnostic test for ZES.

review.stem: Which of the following options is the best management of a low-grade gastric lymphoma of the gastric antrum?
review.explanation: Low-grade MALT lymphoma, essentially a monoclonal proliferation of B cells, presumably arises from a background of chronic gastritis associated with H. pylori. These relatively innocuous tumors then undergo degeneration to high-grade lymphoma, which is the usual variety seen by the surgeon. Remarkably, when the H. pylori is eradicated and the gastritis improves, the low-grade MALT lymphoma often disappears. Thus, low-grade MALT lymphoma is not a surgical lesion. Careful follow-up is necessary particularly in those lesions with a t(11:18) translocation, thought to be a risk factor for a more aggressive MALT lesion.

choiceRationales.A:
Chemotherapy and radiation therapy are commonly used for more aggressive or high-grade lymphomas.
Low-grade MALT (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue) lymphoma of the gastric antrum, associated with H. pylori infection, is typically managed differently. Aggressive treatments like chemotherapy and radiation therapy are not the primary choice for low-grade MALT lymphomas.
choiceRationales.B:
Antrectomy involves the removal of the antrum of the stomach.
Low-grade MALT lymphomas are often responsive to H. pylori eradication therapy, and surgery is not typically the first-line treatment. Antrectomy is not the standard approach for managing low-grade MALT lymphomas.
choiceRationales.C:
Surgical resection, such as wedge resection, may be considered in certain cases.
Surgical resection is generally reserved for cases where conservative measures, such as H. pylori eradication, are not successful, and the lymphoma persists or progresses. However, aggressive surgery like antrectomy is not the primary choice.
choiceRationales.D: Low-grade MALT lymphoma, essentially a monoclonal proliferation of B cells, presumably arises from a background of chronic gastritis associated with H. pylori. Careful follow-up is necessary particularly in those lesions with a t(11:18) translocation, thought to be a risk factor for a more aggressive MALT lesion.

review.stem: A subtotal gastrectomy with D2 dissection performed for stage 3 gastric adenocarcinoma in the antrum includes
review.explanation: Surgical resection is the only curative treatment for gastric cancer, and most patients with clinically resectable locoregional disease should undergo gastric resection. The standard operation for gastric cancer is radical subtotal gastrectomy, which entails ligation of the left and right gastric and gastroepiploic arteries at the origin, as well as the en bloc removal of the distal 75% of the stomach including the pylorus and 2 cm of duodenum, the greater and lesser omentum, and all associated lymphatic tissue. Generally, the surgeon strives for a grossly negative margin of at least 5 cm. More than 15 resected lymph nodes are required for adequate staging, even in the low-risk patient. The operation is deemed an adequate cancer operation provided that tumor-free margins are obtained, at least 15 lymph nodes are removed, and all gross tumor is resected. In the absence of involvement by direct extension, the spleen and pancreatic tail are not removed. Reconstruction is usually done by Billroth I gastrojejunostomy or Roux-en-Y reconstruction.

This type of reconstruction is not typically associated with subtotal gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. choiceRationales.C: Achieving grossly negative margins (R0 resection) is a fundamental goal in gastric cancer surgery. review.stem: Where does the cervical esophagus receive its blood supply primarily?
review.explanation:
The cervical portion of the esophagus receives its main blood supply from the inferior thyroid artery. The thoracic portion receives its blood supply from the bronchial arteries, with 75% of individuals having one right-sided and two left-sided branches. Two esophageal branches arise directly from the aorta. The abdominal portion of the esophagus receives its blood supply from the ascending branch of the left gastric artery and from inferior phrenic arteries (Fig. 25-1).
On entering the wall of the esophagus, the arteries assume a T-shaped division to form a longitudinal plexus, giving rise to an intramural vascular network in the muscular and submucosal layers. As a consequence, the esophagus can be mobilized from the stomach to the level of the aortic arch without fear of devascularization and ischemic necrosis. Caution should be exercised as to the extent of esophageal mobilization in patients who have had a previous thyroidectomy with ligation of the inferior thyroid arteries proximal to the origin of the esophageal branches.

choiceRationales.A: While the superior thyroid artery contributes to the blood supply of the anterior neck, including the thyroid gland and surrounding structures, it is not the primary supplier to the cervical esophagus. Its main role is in the vascularization of the thyroid gland.
choiceRationales.B:

review.explanation:
This is False.
The antireflux mechanism in human beings is composed of three components: A mechanically effective LES, efficient esophageal clearance, and an adequately functioning gastric reservoir. A defect of any one of these three components can lead to increased esophageal exposure to gastric juice and the development of mucosal injury.

choiceRationales.A:

review.stem: Relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi in response to a meal is largely under the control of which hormone?
review.explanation: The sphincter of Oddi is a complex structure that is functionally independent from the duodenal musculature and creates a high-pressure zone between the bile duct and the duodenum. The sphincter of Oddi is about 4 to 6 mm in length and has a basal resting pressure of about 13 mm Hg above the duodenal pressure. On manometry, the sphincter shows phasic contractions with a frequency of about four per minute and an amplitude of 12 to 140 mm Hg. The spontaneous motility of the sphincter of Oddi is regulated by the interstitial cells of Cajal through intrinsic and extrinsic inputs from hormones and neurons acting on the smooth muscle cells. Relaxation occurs with a rise in CCK, leading to diminished amplitude of phasic contractions and reduced basal pressure, allowing increased flow of bile into the duodenum. During fasting, the sphincter of Oddi activity is coordinated with the periodic partial gallbladder emptying and an increase in bile flow that occurs during phase II of the migrating myoelectric motor complexes.

choiceRationales.A: Secretin is a hormone released by the S cells of the duodenum in response to the acidity of chyme. It plays a crucial role in the digestive process by stimulating the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice. However, in the context of the sphincter of Oddi, relaxation is not primarily under the control of secretin. Secretin's main role is in regulating pancreatic and duodenal bicarbonate secretion.
choiceRationales.B: The sphincter of Oddi is a complex structure that is functionally independent from the duodenal musculature and creates a high-pressure zone between the bile duct and the duodenum. The sphincter of Oddi is about 4 to 6 mm in length and has a basal resting pressure of about 13 mm Hg above the duodenal pressure. On manometry, the sphincter shows phasic contractions with a frequency of about four per minute and an amplitude of 12 to 140 mm Hg. The spontaneous motility of the sphincter of Oddi is regulated by the interstitial cells of Cajal through intrinsic and extrinsic inputs from hormones and neurons acting on the smooth muscle cells. Relaxation occurs with a rise in CCK, leading to diminished amplitude of phasic contractions and reduced basal pressure, allowing increased flow of bile into the duodenum. During fasting, the sphincter of Oddi activity is coordinated with the periodic partial gallbladder emptying and an increase in bile flow that occurs during phase II of the migrating myoelectric motor complexes.
choiceRationales.C: Gastrin is a hormone released by the G cells of the stomach. Its primary role is to stimulate the secretion of gastric acid in the stomach. Gastrin does not play a significant role in the relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi.
choiceRationales.D: Motilin is a hormone released by the M cells of the small intestine, particularly in the fasting state. It plays a role in stimulating the migrating motor complex (MMC) in the gastrointestinal tract during fasting. Motilin is not a key regulator of the sphincter of Oddi's relaxation.

B. Cholecystokinin
C. Gastrin
D. Motilin

review.stem: Which factor does NOT increase the risk for the development of gallbladder cancer?
review.explanation: Cancer of the gallbladder is a rare malignancy that occurs predominantly in the elderly. It is two to three times more common in females than males, and the peak incidence is in the seventh decade of life. Cholelithiasis is the most important risk factor for gallbladder carcinoma, and up to 95% of patients with carcinoma of the gallbladder have gallstones. Polypoid lesions of the gallbladder are associated with increased risk of cancer, particularly in polyps >10 mm. The calcified "porcelain" gallbladder is associated with >20% incidence of gallbladder carcinoma. Patients with choledochal cysts have an increased risk of developing cancer anywhere in the biliary tree, but the incidence is highest in the gallbladder. Sclerosing cholangitis, anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction, and exposure to carcinogens (azotoluene, nitrosamines) also are associated with cancer of the gallbladder.

choiceRationales.A: A history of cholelithiasis is a significant risk factor for the development of gallbladder cancer. Up to 95% of patients with gallbladder carcinoma have gallstones. Cholelithiasis is considered the most important risk factor for gallbladder cancer.
choiceRationales.B: Female gender is, in fact, associated with an increased risk of gallbladder cancer. The malignancy is two to three times more common in females than males, and the peak incidence is in the seventh decade of life.
choiceRationales.C: Cancer of the gallbladder is a rare malignancy that occurs predominantly in the elderly. It is two to three times more common in females than males, and the peak incidence is in the seventh decade of life. Sclerosing cholangitis, anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction, and exposure to carcinogens (azotoluene, nitrosamines) also are associated with cancer of the gallbladder.
choiceRationales.D: Gallbladder polyps, especially those larger than 10 mm, are associated with an increased risk of gallbladder cancer. Polypoid lesions of the gallbladder, particularly larger polyps, are mentioned as a risk factor for the development of cancer in the gallbladder.

review.stem: A closed-loop obstruction is particularly dangerous because:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The obstructive segment is not apparent on imaging studies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intraluminal pressure rises high enough to cause ischemia and necrosis

review.explanation: A closed loop obstruction, in which an intestinal segment is obstructed both proximally and distally, such as in a volvulus, is particularly dangerous because intraluminal pressure rises quickly and can cause venous congestion and arterial obstruction, leading to necrosis of the intestinal wall and perforation. It classically presents with "pain out of proportion to the physical exam," and is usually apparent on a CT scan, which frequently shows a U-shaped or C-shaped dilated bowel loop associated with a radial distribution of mesenteric vessels converging toward a torsion point.

choiceRationales.A: A closed-loop obstruction is typically apparent on imaging studies, especially on a CT scan. In this type of obstruction, the affected intestinal segment is obstructed both proximally and distally, leading to characteristic findings on imaging such as a U-shaped or C-shaped dilated bowel loop. The obstruction is usually visible, and the imaging helps in diagnosing the condition.
choiceRationales.B: A closed loop obstruction, in which an intestinal segment is obstructed both proximally and distally, such as in a volvulus, is particularly dangerous because intraluminal pressure rises quickly and can cause venous congestion and arterial obstruction, leading to necrosis of the intestinal wall and perforation. It classically presents with "pain out of proportion to the physical exam," and is usually apparent on a CT scan, which frequently shows a U-shaped or C-shaped dilated bowel loop associated with a radial distribution of mesenteric vessels converging toward a torsion point.
choiceRationales.C: Closed-loop obstructions are not typically painless. In fact, they often present with severe abdominal pain, which is described as "pain out of proportion to the physical exam." This is due to the rapid rise in intraluminal pressure and the potential for ischemia and necrosis.
choiceRationales.D: While bacterial overgrowth can occur in the setting of intestinal obstruction, closed-loop obstructions are more directly associated with the risk of ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. If perforation occurs, bacterial peritonitis can lead to sepsis, but the primary concern is the mechanical complications and ischemic damage.

Removal of the appendix has been associated with a protective effect of which of the following?

It has been suggested that appendectomy is associated with increased C. difficile infections and increased subsequent cancer (colon, esophageal) as a result of microbial alteration, although this is currently unproven. The protective effect of an early appendectomy against the development of ulcerative colitis has been proposed to be mechanistically linked to the release of dimeric forms of IgA from plasma B cells and the Th2 response mediated by IL-13-producing natural killer T cells.

review.explanation:
During pregnancy, the breast goes through significant growth and maturation processes due to hormonal stimulation. This leads to the accumulation of immune cells and changes in the structure of the breast tissue. The ducts and alveoli, which are small sac-like structures, undergo development. This development is not always uniform, and variations in the degree of development can occur within the same lobule.
After childbirth, further enlargement of the breasts occurs as the alveolar epithelium undergoes hypertrophy (increase in size) and accumulates secretory products in the ducts. The alveolar epithelium contains various components such as endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, Golgi complexes, and lysosomes. It produces two main substances: the protein component of milk, which is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (exocrine secretion), and the lipid component of milk, which forms as free lipid droplets in the cytoplasm (apocrine secretion).
The milk produced in the first few days after childbirth is called colostrum. It has low lipid content but contains significant quantities of antibodies.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is associated with pregnancy and lactation. During pregnancy, the breast undergoes changes in preparation for lactation. The alveolar epithelium produces secretory products, and these accumulate in the ducts. This accumulation is part of the normal physiological changes associated with pregnancy and breastfeeding.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is accurate. During pregnancy, there is an accumulation of immune cells in the breast tissue. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils are among the immune cells that are part of the breast tissue changes during pregnancy. These cells play a role in the immunological aspects of lactation.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is accurate. Enlargement of breast alveoli occurs during pregnancy as part of the developmental changes in preparation for lactation. The alveoli increase in size, and the alveolar epithelium undergoes hypertrophy to accommodate the production and storage of milk.

During pregnancy, the breast goes through significant growth and maturation processes due to hormonal stimulation. This leads to the accumulation of immune cells and changes in the structure of the breast tissue. The ducts and alveoli, which are small sac-like structures, undergo development. This development is not always uniform, and variations in the degree of development can occur within the same lobule.
After childbirth, further enlargement of the breasts occurs as the alveolar epithelium undergoes hypertrophy (increase in size) and accumulates secretory products in the ducts. The alveolar epithelium contains various components such as endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, Golgi complexes, and lysosomes. It produces two main substances: the protein component of milk, which is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (exocrine secretion), and the lipid component of milk, which forms as free lipid droplets in the cytoplasm (apocrine secretion).
The milk produced in the first few days after childbirth is called colostrum. It has low lipid content but contains significant quantities of antibodies.

review.stem: Exposure of the skin to thermal extremes disrupts its primary function as a barrier to heat loss, evaporation and microbial invasion. Which are is MOST amenable to salvage by resuscitative and wound management techniques following thermal injury?
review.explanation: The management of thermal wounds is initially guided by the concept of three distinct zones of injury. The focus of thermal injury that has already undergone necrosis is known as the zone of coagulation. Well outside the zone of coagulation is the zone of hyperemia, which exhibits signs of inflammation but will likely remain viable. In between these two zones is a zone of stasis with questionable tissue viability, and it is this area at which proper burn care can salvage viable tissue and decrease the extent of injury.

choiceRationales.A: The zone of coagulation is the area of thermal injury that has undergone irreversible damage and necrosis. It is the most central region of the burn wound, and the tissue in this zone is nonviable. Salvaging tissue in the zone of coagulation is not feasible, as the damage is irreversible. The focus of management in this area is wound care and preventing infection.
choiceRationales.B: The management of thermal wounds is initially guided by the concept of three distinct zones of injury. The focus of thermal injury that has already undergone necrosis is known as the zone of coagulation. Well outside the zone of coagulation is the zone of hyperemia, which exhibits signs of inflammation but will likely remain viable. In between these two zones is a zone of stasis with questionable tissue viability, and it is this area at which proper burn care can salvage viable tissue and decrease the extent of injury.
choiceRationales.C: The zone of hyperemia is the outermost area surrounding the burn wound. This zone exhibits signs of inflammation but is expected to remain viable. It represents a zone of increased blood flow as a response to the injury. The tissue in the zone of hyperemia is not compromised and is considered salvageable with proper wound care.
choiceRationales.D: The term "zone of scalding" is not typically used in the context of burn classification. Thermal injuries are commonly described in terms of the zones of coagulation, stasis, and hyperemia.

review.stem: The clinician observes and treats injury to the skin based on degree of presentation. Following caustic injury to the skin with an alkaline agent, the affected area should be initially be treated with a .

choices.label: B
choices.text: Running water or saline for 30 minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Running water or saline for 2 hours

review.explanation: Treatment for acidic or alkaline chemical burns is first and foremost centered around dilution of the offending agent, typically using distilled water or saline for 30 minutes for acidic burns and 2 hours for alkaline injuries. Attempting to neutralize the offending agent is typically discouraged, as it does not offer an advantage over dilution, and the neutralization reaction could be exothermic, increasing the amount of tissue damage. After the removal of the caustic agent, the burn is treated like other burns and is based on the depth of tissue injury.

choiceRationales.A: Using a neutralizing agent is generally discouraged in the treatment of chemical burns, whether caused by acidic or alkaline substances. Neutralization reactions can be exothermic and may worsen tissue damage. The primary and immediate goal is to dilute and remove the caustic substance. Neutralizing agents may not be effective and can lead to additional complications.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is accurate for acidic burns, but not for alkaline burns. For an alkaline caustic injury, the recommended duration for irrigation is typically longer, around 2 hours. Prolonged irrigation helps in diluting and removing the alkaline substance from the affected area.
choiceRationales.C: Treatment for acidic or alkaline chemical burns is first and foremost centered around dilution of the offending agent, typically using distilled water or saline for 30 minutes for acidic burns and 2 hours for alkaline injuries. Attempting to neutralize the offending agent is typically discouraged, as it does not offer an advantage over dilution, and the neutralization reaction could be exothermic, increasing the amount of tissue damage. After the removal of the caustic agent, the burn is treated like other burns and is based on the depth of tissue injury.
choiceRationales.D: Topical emollients and oral analgesics are not the primary interventions for caustic injuries. The immediate focus is on thorough irrigation to remove the caustic substance. Subsequent management may involve topical treatments and pain control, but the initial step is prolonged irrigation.

review.stem: To which lymphatic basin will a cutaneous malignancy of the anterior abdominal wall 2 inches above the umbilicus drain?
review.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the anterior abdominal wall is principally to the axillary nodal basin and the inguinal nodal basin. The area of demarcation is roughly the arcuate line (semilunar line of Douglas) at the level of the anterior iliac spine. Malignancies above the arcuate line drain superiorly, and those below the line drain inferiorly.

choiceRationales.A: The inguinal lymphatic basin is one of the drainage pathways for the anterior abdominal wall. Malignancies below the arcuate line (semilunar line of Douglas), which is approximately at the level of the anterior iliac spine, tend to drain into the inguinal nodes. However, a cutaneous malignancy 2 inches above the umbilicus, being above this demarcation, would primarily drain superiorly.
choiceRationales.B: The umbilical region does have lymphatic drainage, but malignancies above the arcuate line, including the area 2 inches above the umbilicus, are more likely to drain superiorly to the axillary nodes.
choiceRationales.C: The lymphatic drainage of the anterior abdominal wall is principally to the axillary nodal basin and the inguinal nodal basin. The area of demarcation is roughly the arcuate line (semilunar line of Douglas) at the level of the anterior iliac spine. Malignancies above the arcuate line drain superiorly, and those below the line drain inferiorly.
choiceRationales.D: Retroperitoneal lymph nodes are not typically involved in the drainage of cutaneous malignancies of the anterior abdominal wall. The primary drainage routes for these malignancies are the inguinal and axillary lymphatic basins.

review.stem: Epidemiologic studies have identified risk factors that may predispose to a hernia. Which two types of collagen are found in a decreased ratio of the skin of inguinal hernia patients?
review.explanation: Epidemiological studies have identified risk factors that may predispose individuals to a hernia. Microscopic examination of the skin of inguinal hernia patients demonstrated significantly decreased ratios of type I to type III collagen. Type III collagen does not contribute to wound tensile strength as significantly as type I collagen. Additional analyses revealed disaggregated collagen tracts with decreased collagen fiber density in hernia patients' skin. Collagen disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are also associated with an increased incidence of hernia formation (Table 37-4). Recent studies have found an association between concentrations of extracellular matrix elements and hernia formation. Although a significant amount of work remains to elucidate the biological nature of hernias, current evidence suggests they have a multifactorial etiology with both environmental and hereditary influences.

choiceRationales.A: The correct answer is not Types II and III. The decreased ratio of collagen types found in the skin of inguinal hernia patients is specifically related to Types I and III collagen.
choiceRationales.B: The correct answer is not Types I and II. The altered collagen ratio associated with inguinal hernias involves Types I and III collagen.
choiceRationales.C: The correct answer is not Types III and VI. The primary focus in inguinal hernia patients is on the decreased ratio of Type I to Type III collagen in the skin.
choiceRationales.D: Epidemiological studies have identified risk factors that may predispose individuals to a hernia. Microscopic examination of the skin of inguinal hernia patients demonstrated significantly decreased ratios of type I to type III collagen. Type III collagen does not contribute to wound tensile strength as significantly as type I collagen. Additional analyses revealed disaggregated collagen tracts with decreased collagen fiber density in hernia patients' skin. Collagen disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are also associated with an increased incidence of hernia formation (Table 37-4). Recent studies have found an association between concentrations of extracellular matrix elements and hernia formation. Although a significant amount of work remains to elucidate the biological nature of hernias, current evidence suggests they have a multifactorial etiology with both environmental and hereditary influences.

choiceRationales.A: Children exposed to the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 did not demonstrate an increased incidence of follicular thyroid cancer. The primary association with radiation exposure, particularly in children, is with papillary thyroid cancer.
choiceRationales.B: Anaplastic thyroid cancer is a highly aggressive and undifferentiated form of thyroid cancer. review.stem: A trauma patient arrives following a stab wound to the left chest with systolic blood pressure 85 mmHg, which improves slightly with IV fluid resuscitation. Chest X-ray demonstrates clear lung fields. What is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tube thoracostomy of the left chest

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computed tomography scan of the chest

choices.label: C
choices.text: Focused abdominal sonography for trauma examination

review.explanation: During the circulation section of the primary survey, four life-threatening injuries must be identified promptly: (1) massive hemothorax, (2) cardiac tamponade, (3) massive hemoperitoneum, and (4) mechanically unstable pelvic fractures with bleeding. In this patient, hemothorax is unlikely given a normal chest X-ray; thus, hemoperitoneum and cardiac tamponade should be suspected. Cardiac tamponade occurs most commonly after penetrating thoracic wounds, although occasionally blunt rupture of the heart, particularly the atrial appendage, is seen. Acutely, less than 100 mL of pericardial blood may cause pericardial tamponade. The classic Beck's triad—dilated neck veins, muffled heart tones, and a decline in arterial pressure—is usually not appreciated in the trauma bay because of the noisy environment and associated hypovolemia. Diagnosis is best achieved by bedside ultrasound of the pericardium, which is one of the four views of the FAST examination.

choiceRationales.A: Tube thoracostomy is indicated in patients with suspected or confirmed hemothorax or tension pneumothorax. In this case, the chest X-ray demonstrates clear lung fields, making hemothorax less likely. Tube thoracostomy would be more appropriate if there were signs of tension pneumothorax or if the patient's clinical condition deteriorates.
choiceRationales.B: While a chest CT scan provides detailed information about chest injuries, in the initial assessment of a trauma patient with hypotension and a stab wound to the left chest, immediate intervention to identify and manage life-threatening conditions is crucial. Chest CT may be considered after the primary survey and initial stabilization.
choiceRationales.C: During the circulation section of the primary survey, four life-threatening injuries must be identified promptly: (1) massive hemothorax, (2) cardiac tamponade, (3) massive hemoperitoneum, and (4) mechanically unstable pelvic fractures with bleeding. In this patient, hemothorax is unlikely given a normal chest X-ray; thus, hemoperitoneum and cardiac tamponade should be suspected. Cardiac tamponade occurs most commonly after penetrating thoracic wounds, although occasionally blunt rupture of the heart, particularly the atrial appendage, is seen. Acutely, less than 100 mL of pericardial blood may cause pericardial tamponade. The classic Beck's triad—dilated neck veins, muffled heart tones, and a decline in arterial pressure—is usually not appreciated in the trauma bay because of the noisy environment and associated hypovolemia. Diagnosis is best achieved by bedside ultrasound of the pericardium, which is one of the four views of the FAST examination.
choiceRationales.D: A pelvic X-ray is not the most appropriate next step in the evaluation of a trauma patient with a stab wound to the left chest and hypotension. The primary focus should be on identifying life-threatening thoracic and abdominal injuries.

review.stem: The most common malignant tumor of the brain is
review.explanation: Astrocytoma is the most common primary central nervous system (CNS) neoplasm. The term glioma is often used to refer to astrocytomas specifically, excluding other glial tumors. Astrocytomas are graded from I to IV. Grades I and II are referred to as low-grade astrocytoma or low-grade glioma, grade III as anaplastic astrocytoma, and grade IV as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). Prognosis varies significantly between grades I/II, III, and IV, but not between I and II. The median survival is 8 years after diagnosis with a low-grade tumor, 2 to 3 years with an anaplastic astrocytoma, and roughly 1 year with a GBM. GBMs account for almost two-thirds of all astrocytomas, anaplastic astrocytomas account for two-thirds of the remaining cases, and low-grade astrocytomas make up the rest. Figure 42-3 demonstrates the typical appearance of a GBM.

choiceRationales.A: Ganglioglioma is a rare type of brain tumor that contains both neural (ganglion cells) and glial (glioma) components. It is considered a low-grade tumor and often occurs in the temporal lobes of the brain. While it is a type of brain tumor, it is not the most common malignant tumor of the brain.
choiceRationales.B: Astrocytoma is the most common primary central nervous system (CNS) neoplasm. The term glioma is often used to refer to astrocytomas specifically, excluding other glial tumors. Astrocytomas are graded from I to IV. Grades I and II are referred to as low-grade astrocytoma or low-grade glioma, grade III as anaplastic astrocytoma, and grade IV as glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). Prognosis varies significantly between grades I/II, III, and IV, but not between I and II. The median survival is 8 years after diagnosis with a low-grade tumor, 2 to 3 years with an anaplastic astrocytoma, and roughly 1 year with a GBM. GBMs account for almost two-thirds of all astrocytomas, anaplastic astrocytomas account for two-thirds of the remaining cases, and low-grade astrocytomas make up the rest. Figure 42-3 demonstrates the typical appearance of a GBM.
choiceRationales.C: Ependymoma is a type of brain tumor that arises from ependymal cells lining the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. It is more common in children than adults. While ependymomas can be malignant, they are not as common as astrocytomas.
choiceRationales.D: Teratoma is a type of tumor that can contain tissues from all three germ layers (endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm). In the context of the brain, teratomas are extremely rare. They are more commonly found in the ovaries and testes.

A. Ganglioglioma
B. Astrocytoma
C. Ependymoma
D. Teratoma

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: A patient in the ICU has been on ventilator support for 3 weeks. He has new onset of elevated WBC count, fever, and consolidation seen on chest X-ray. What is an appropriate next step?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exchange endotracheal tube and change respiratory circuit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start treatment with empiric penicillin G

review.explanation: Prolonged mechanical ventilation is associated with nosocomial pneumonia. These patients present with more severe disease, are more likely to be infected with drug-resistant pathogens, and suffer increased mortality compared to patients who develop community-acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of pneumonia is established by the presence of purulent sputum, an elevated leukocyte count, fever, and new chest x-ray abnormalities such as consolidation. The presence of two of the clinical findings, plus chest X-ray findings, significantly increases the likelihood of pneumonia. Consideration should be given to performing bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain samples for Gram's stain and culture. Some authors advocate quantitative cultures as a means to identify a threshold for diagnosis. Surgical patients should be weaned from mechanical ventilation as soon as feasible, based on oxygenation and inspiratory effort, as prolonged mechanical ventilation increases the risk of nosocomial pneumonia.

choiceRationales.A: While chest CT can provide detailed information about lung pathology, in the context of a ventilated ICU patient with new-onset symptoms, the initial step is often a chest X-ray. Chest X-ray is a quicker and more practical tool for the initial assessment of lung consolidation in a critically ill patient.
choiceRationales.B: Changing the endotracheal tube and respiratory circuit may be considered as part of infection control measures, but it doesn't directly address the diagnostic or therapeutic aspects of the suspected pneumonia. This step may be taken in conjunction with other interventions.
choiceRationales.C: The statement is incorrect. Empiric treatment for pneumonia should be based on the likely pathogens involved, and penicillin G alone may not cover the spectrum of organisms commonly associated with ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). Broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria are often initiated pending culture results.
choiceRationales.D: Prolonged mechanical ventilation is associated with nosocomial pneumonia. These patients present with more severe disease, are more likely to be infected with drug-resistant pathogens, and suffer increased mortality compared to patients who develop community-acquired pneumonia. The diagnosis of pneumonia is established by the presence of purulent sputum, an elevated leukocyte count, fever, and new chest x-ray abnormalities such as consolidation. The presence of two of the clinical findings, plus chest X-ray findings, significantly increases the likelihood of pneumonia. Consideration should be given to performing bronchoalveolar lavage to obtain samples for Gram's stain and culture. Some authors advocate quantitative cultures as a means to identify a threshold for diagnosis. Surgical patients should be weaned from mechanical ventilation as soon as feasible, based on oxygenation and inspiratory effort, as prolonged mechanical ventilation increases the risk of nosocomial pneumonia.

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: Possible exposure to anthrax should be initially treated with:
review.explanation: Inhalational anthrax develops after a 1- to 6-day incubation period, with nonspecific symptoms including malaise, myalgia, and fever. Over a short period of time, these symptoms worsen, with the development of respiratory distress, chest pain, and diaphoresis. Characteristic chest radiographic findings include a widened mediastinum and pleural effusions. A key aspect in establishing the diagnosis is eliciting an exposure history. Rapid antigen tests are currently under development for the identification of this gram-positive rod. Postexposure prophylaxis consists of the administration of either ciprofloxacin or doxycycline. If an isolate is demonstrated to be penicillin-sensitive, the patient should be switched to amoxicillin. Inhalational exposure followed by the development of symptoms is associated with a high mortality rate. Treatment options include combination therapy with ciprofloxacin, clindamycin, and rifampin; clindamycin added to block production of toxin, while rifampin penetrates into the central nervous system and intracellular locations.

choiceRationales.A: Colistin is an antibiotic primarily used for treating infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. It is not the recommended first-line treatment for anthrax exposure. In the context of possible anthrax exposure, other antibiotics with specific activity against Bacillus anthracis are preferred.
choiceRationales.B: Inhalational anthrax develops after a 1- to 6-day incubation period, with nonspecific symptoms including malaise, myalgia, and fever. Over a short period of time, these symptoms worsen, with the development of respiratory distress, chest pain, and diaphoresis. Characteristic chest radiographic findings include a widened mediastinum and pleural effusions. A key aspect in establishing the diagnosis is eliciting an exposure history. Rapid antigen tests are currently under development for the identification of this gram-positive rod. Postexposure prophylaxis consists of the administration of either ciprofloxacin or doxycycline. If an isolate is demonstrated to be penicillin-sensitive, the patient should be switched to amoxicillin. Inhalational exposure followed by the development of symptoms is associated with a high mortality rate. Treatment options include combination therapy with ciprofloxacin, clindamycin, and rifampin; clindamycin added to block production of toxin, while rifampin penetrates into the central nervous system and intracellular locations.
choiceRationales.C: While amoxicillin is an effective antibiotic against many bacteria, it is not the first-line choice for post-exposure prophylaxis in anthrax. Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are more commonly recommended due to their specific activity against Bacillus anthracis.
choiceRationales.D: Observation alone without antibiotic prophylaxis is not the recommended approach in the case of suspected anthrax exposure. The high mortality rate associated with inhalational anthrax underscores the importance of prompt initiation of appropriate antibiotics for postexposure prophylaxis.

A. Colistin
B. Ciprofloxacin
C. Amoxicillin
D. Observation

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: What is the MOST common intradural extramedullary tumor in children?
review.explanation: Astrocytomas are the most common intramedullary tumors in children, although they also occur in adults. They may occur at all levels, although more often in the cervical cord. The tumor may interfere with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-containing central canal of the spinal cord, leading to a dilated central canal referred to as syringomyelia (syrinx).

choiceRationales.A: Astrocytomas are the most common intramedullary tumors in children, although they also occur in adults. They may occur at all levels, although more often in the cervical cord. The tumor may interfere with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-containing central canal of the spinal cord, leading to a dilated central canal referred to as syringomyelia (syrinx).
choiceRationales.B: Ependymomas are intramedullary tumors that can occur in the spinal cord. They arise from ependymal cells lining the central canal. While less common than astrocytomas, ependymomas are significant contributors to intradural spinal cord tumors in children.
choiceRationales.C: Dermoid tumors are typically extramedullary and are not commonly found within the substance of the spinal cord. These tumors contain tissues such as hair, skin, and sometimes teeth and are usually located in the sacral region.
choiceRationales.D: Similar to dermoid tumors, teratomas are usually extramedullary and consist of tissues from multiple germ cell layers. They are not as commonly found within the spinal cord itself.

review.stem: Advantages of laparoscopic adrenalectomy compared with open adrenalectomy include all of the following, EXCEPT:
review.explanation: Laparoscopic (videoscopic) approaches to adrenalectomy have been shown to be advantageous for several outcomes, including wound complications, analgesic use, and length of hospital stay. These advantages are balanced against adverse considerations, including length of operative time and cost.

choiceRationales.A: Laparoscopic (videoscopic) approaches to adrenalectomy have been shown to be advantageous for several outcomes, including wound complications, analgesic use, and length of hospital stay. These advantages are balanced against adverse considerations, including length of operative time and cost.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is accurate. Laparoscopic procedures generally result in smaller incisions, which can lead to a decreased incidence of wound infections compared to the larger incisions required in open surgery.
choiceRationales.C: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is associated with decreased narcotic analgesic use. The minimally invasive nature of laparoscopic surgery contributes to reduced postoperative pain, allowing for better pain control with fewer narcotic medications.
choiceRationales.D: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is associated with a decreased length of hospital stay. Patients undergoing laparoscopic procedures typically recover more quickly, experience less postoperative pain, and are discharged earlier than those undergoing open surgery.

review.stem: All of the following are true concerning priapism EXCEPT

choices.label: A
choices.text: Treatment may require injection of phenylephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Priapism is defined as persistent erection or 4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low flow priapism can be confirmed with a penile blood gas determination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Etiologic factors include sickle cell disease, malignancy, total parenteral nutrition, penile shaft fractures.

review.explanation: Priapism is a persistent erection for more than 4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation. Risk factors include sickle cell disease or trait, malignancy, medications, cocaine abuse, certain antidepressants, and total parenteral nutrition. Low-flow priapism can be confirmed with a penile blood gas of the cavernosal bodies demonstrating hypoxic, acidotic blood. Injection of phenylephrine (up to 200 mg in 20 mL normal saline) into the corporal bodies may be required.

choiceRationales.A: This statement is true. Phenylephrine is a common intervention for priapism, particularly in cases of ischemic or low-flow priapism. It works by inducing smooth muscle contraction in the corpora cavernosa, which helps evacuate stagnant blood and relieve the persistent erection.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is accurate. Priapism is defined as a persistent and often painful erection lasting for more than 4 hours, unrelated to sexual stimulation or desire. It is a urologic emergency that requires prompt evaluation and intervention.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is true. Low-flow priapism, also known as ischemic priapism, is characterized by a reduction in blood flow to the penis. Confirmation can be achieved through a penile blood gas determination, which typically shows hypoxic and acidotic blood in the cavernosal bodies.
choiceRationales.D: Priapism is a persistent erection for more than 4 hours unrelated to sexual stimulation. Risk factors include sickle cell disease or trait, malignancy, medications, cocaine abuse, certain antidepressants, and total parenteral nutrition. Low-flow priapism can be confirmed with a penile blood gas of the cavernosal bodies demonstrating hypoxic, acidotic blood. Injection of phenylephrine (up to 200 mg in 20 mL normal saline) into the corporal bodies may be required.

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) have regulatory roles in all of the following, EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visual acuity in low-light conditions (“night vision”)

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speed of muscle contraction and relaxation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hypoxia and hypercapnia drives of the respiratory center in the brain

review.explanation: Thyroid hormones are responsible for maintaining the normal hypoxic and hypercapnic drive in the respiratory center of the brain and regulating cholesterol synthesis and degradation. They also regulate bone and protein turnover, the speed of muscle contraction and regulation, gastrointestinal motility, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and intestinal glucose absorption, but they are not regulators of auditory acuity.

review.stem: Which of the following statements is NOT TRUE when a patient with hemorrhagic shock is resuscitated using an intravenous colloid solution rather than lactated ringer solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colloid solutions may bind to the ionized fraction of serum calcium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating levels of immunoglobulins are decreased

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extracellular fluid volume deficit is restored

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endogenous production of albumin is decreased

review.explanation: Because of higher osmotic pressure, colloid solutions draw extracellular fluid into the vascular space, increasing the extracellular fluid deficit. In addition, the ionized fraction of serum calcium is decreased, circulating levels of immunoglobulin drop, and the reaction to tetanus toxoid given to the patient suffering from major trauma is decreased. choiceRationales.A: This statement is true. Colloid solutions, especially those containing negatively charged particles, can bind to the ionized fraction of serum calcium, potentially affecting the ionized calcium levels in the blood.

choiceRationales.C: Because of higher osmotic pressure, colloid solutions draw extracellular fluid into the vascular space, increasing the extracellular fluid deficit. In addition, the ionized fraction of serum calcium is decreased, circulating levels of immunoglobulin drop, and the reaction to tetanus toxoid given to the patient suffering from major trauma is decreased. Endogenous production of albumin also decreases. Colloid resuscitation is no more effective than crystalloid resuscitation, and it is more expensive. Furthermore, its use in bleeding trauma patients is associated with an increased risk of death.
choiceRationales.D: This statement is true. The use of colloid solutions, particularly those containing exogenous albumin, can lead to a decrease in the endogenous production of albumin by the liver.

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: Which of the following occur as a result of epinephrine and norepinephrine?
review.explanation: Epinephrine and norepinephrine have a profound impact on cellular metabolism. Hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, skeletal muscle protein breakdown, and adipose tissue lipolysis are increased by catecholamines. Cortisol, glucagon, and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) also contribute to catabolism during shock. Epinephrine induces further release of glucagon while inhibiting the pancreatic β-cell release of insulin. The result is a catabolic state with glucose mobilization, hyperglycemia, protein breakdown, negative nitrogen balance, lipolysis, and insulin resistance during shock and injury. The relative underuse of glucose by peripheral tissues preserves it for the glucose-dependent organs, such as the heart and brain.

choiceRationales.A: The release of epinephrine and norepinephrine inhibits lipogenesis. Instead, catecholamines promote lipolysis, the breakdown of stored fats into free fatty acids, which can be utilized as an energy source.
choiceRationales.B: This statement is not accurate. Epinephrine and norepinephrine contribute to hyperglycemia by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis (conversion of glycogen to glucose) and gluconeogenesis (production of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources).
choiceRationales.C: Catecholamines, particularly epinephrine, reduce insulin sensitivity. They counteract the effects of insulin, promoting glucose mobilization and preventing excessive glucose uptake by peripheral tissues.
choiceRationales.D: Epinephrine and norepinephrine have a profound impact on cellular metabolism. Hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis, skeletal muscle protein breakdown, and adipose tissue lipolysis are increased by catecholamines. Cortisol, glucagon, and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) also contribute to catabolism during shock. Epinephrine induces further release of glucagon while inhibiting the pancreatic β-cell release of insulin. The result is a catabolic state with glucose mobilization, hyperglycemia, protein breakdown, negative nitrogen balance, lipolysis, and insulin resistance during shock and injury. The relative underuse of glucose by peripheral tissues preserves it for the glucose-dependent organs, such as the heart and brain.

review.subject: surgery
review.stem: Which factor does NOT influence the development of surgical site infections?
review.explanation: SSIs are infections of the tissues, organs, or spaces exposed by surgeons during the performance of an invasive procedure. SSIs are classified into incisional and organ/space infections, and the former are further subclassified into superficial (limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue) and deep incisional categories. The development of SSIs is related to three factors: (a) the degree of microbial contamination of the wound during surgery; (b) the duration of the procedure; and (c) host factors such as diabetes, malnutrition, obesity, immune suppression, and a number of other underlying disease states. By definition, an incisional SSI has occurred if a surgical wound drains purulent material or if the surgeon judges it to be infected and opens it.

choiceRationales.A: The duration of the surgical procedure is a factor influencing the development of surgical site infections (SSIs). Prolonged surgeries are associated with an increased risk of infections, possibly due to longer exposure of tissues to the environment and a higher likelihood of microbial contamination.
choiceRationales.B: The degree of microbial contamination is a significant factor in the development of SSIs. Contaminated or dirty surgical procedures, where the risk of infection is higher due to the presence of microorganisms, increase the likelihood of SSIs.
choiceRationales.C: Malnutrition is a recognized risk factor for the development of SSIs. Adequate nutritional status is crucial for optimal wound healing and immune function. Malnourished individuals may have compromised immune responses, leading to an increased susceptibility to infections.
choiceRationales.D: SSIs are infections of the tissues, organs, or spaces exposed by surgeons during the performance of an invasive procedure. SSIs are classified into incisional and organ/space infections, and the former are further subclassified into superficial (limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue) and deep incisional categories. review.stem: Which of the following is TRUE about antidiuretic hormone production in injured patients?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acts as a potent mesenteric vasoconstrictor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Levels fall to normal within 2 to 3 days of the initial insult

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mediates secretion by the renin-angiotensin system

review.explanation: The pituitary gland also releases vasopressin or ADH in response to hypovolemia, changes in circulating blood volume sensed by baroreceptors and left atrial stretch receptors, and increased plasma osmolality detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors. Epinephrine, angiotensin II, pain, and hyperglycemia increase the production of ADH. ADH levels remain elevated for about 1 week after the initial insult, depending on the severity and persistence of the hemodynamic abnormalities. ADH acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct of the nephron to increase water permeability, decrease water and sodium losses, and preserve intravascular volume. Also known as arginine vasopressin, ADH acts as a potent mesenteric vasoconstrictor, shunting circulating blood away from the splanchnic organs during hypovolemia. This may contribute to intestinal ischemia and predispose to intestinal mucosal barrier dysfunction in shock states. Vasopressin also increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and hepatic glycolysis.

choiceRationales.A: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also known as vasopressin, increases hepatic gluconeogenesis. In the context of injured patients, ADH contributes to increased glucose production by the liver. This effect is part of the hormone's role in maintaining blood glucose levels during stress and injury.
choiceRationales.B: The pituitary gland also releases vasopressin or ADH in response to hypovolemia, changes in circulating blood volume sensed by baroreceptors and left atrial stretch receptors, and increased plasma osmolality detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors. Epinephrine, angiotensin II, pain, and hyperglycemia increase the production of ADH. ADH levels remain elevated for about 1 week after the initial insult, depending on the severity and persistence of the hemodynamic abnormalities. This may contribute to intestinal ischemia and predispose to intestinal mucosal barrier dysfunction in shock states. Vasopressin also increases hepatic gluconeogenesis and hepatic glycolysis.
choiceRationales.C: This statement is not accurate. ADH levels can remain elevated for about 1 week after the initial insult, depending on the severity and duration of hemodynamic abnormalities. The hormone plays a crucial role in the body's response to hypovolemia and stress.
choiceRationales.D: ADH does not mediate secretion by the renin-angiotensin system. review.stem: Which of the following definitions is INCORRECT?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free flap: flaps that are completely detached from the body prior to their reimplantation with microvascular anastomoses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flap composition: Description of the tissue components within flap

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pedicle: Bridge of tissue that remains between a flap and its source; blood vessels that nourish a flap

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flap contiguity: the position of a flap relative to its recipient bed

review.explanation: The composition of a flap describes its tissue components. The contiguity of a flap describes its position relative to its source. Distant flaps are transferred from a different anatomical region to the defect. They may remain attached to the source anatomical region (pedicle flaps) or may be transferred as free flaps by microsurgery. These are completely detached from the body, and their blood supply is restored by microvascular anastomoses to recipient vessels near the defect. The term pedicle was originally used to describe a bridge of tissue that remained between a flap and its source, similar to how a peninsula remains attached to its mainland. However, as knowledge of flap blood supply and (micro)vascular anatomy has improved over the years, the term pedicle has increasingly been reserved for describing the blood vessels that nourish the flap.

choiceRationales.A: This definition is correct. Free flaps refer to flaps that are completely detached from the body prior to their reimplantation. Microvascular anastomoses are used to restore blood supply.
choiceRationales.B: This definition is correct. Flap composition refers to the description of the tissue components within a flap. This can include skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, or other structures, depending on the type of flap.
choiceRationales.C: This definition is somewhat correct. The pedicle was traditionally described as a bridge of tissue that remains between a flap and its source. However, with advancements in microvascular surgery, the term "pedicle" is more commonly used to refer to the blood vessels that nourish a flap. So, while the traditional definition is mentioned, the contemporary understanding emphasizes the vascular aspect.
choiceRationales.D: The composition of a flap describes its tissue components. The contiguity of a flap describes its position relative to its source. Distant flaps are transferred from a different anatomical region to the defect. They may remain attached to the source anatomical region (pedicle flaps) or may be transferred as free flaps by microsurgery. These are completely detached from the body, and their blood supply is restored by microvascular anastomoses to recipient vessels near the defect. The term pedicle was originally used to describe a bridge of tissue that remained between a flap and its source, similar to how a peninsula remains attached to its mainland. However, as knowledge of flap blood supply and (micro)vascular anatomy has improved over the years, the term pedicle has increasingly been reserved for describing the blood vessels that nourish the flap.

review.stem: All hand infections EXCEPT which of the following require surgical management?
review.explanation: All hand infections other than cellulitis will require surgical management. Clinical examination, particularly noting the area of greatest tenderness and/or inflammation, is the single most useful diagnostic tool to localize any purulence requiring drainage.

choiceRationales.A: Osteomyelitis, an infection of the bone, often requires surgical management. This is especially true in the hand, where the presence of purulent material within bone spaces may necessitate drainage and debridement. Surgical intervention is crucial to remove infected tissue and promote healing.
choiceRationales.B: A felon is an infection of the pulp space of the fingertip. It typically presents with intense pain and swelling. Incision and drainage are commonly performed for felons to alleviate pressure and drain purulent material, providing relief and promoting recovery.
choiceRationales.C: Paronychia, an infection of the soft tissue around the nail, may be managed with incision and drainage in certain cases. The decision for surgical intervention depends on the severity of the infection and the presence of abscess formation.
choiceRationales.D: All hand infections other than cellulitis will require surgical management. Clinical examination, particularly noting the area of greatest tenderness and/or inflammation, is the single most useful diagnostic tool to localize any purulence requiring drainage.
